blocks.subject: entry:book/gen
blocks.body:
Genesis tells two stories. Chapters 1–11 cover the whole world: creation, the first humans, the spread of violence, the flood and Babel. Chapters 12–50 narrow to one family, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, through whom God promises to bless "all families of the earth" (Gen 12:3).

The book was written against the background of Ancient Near Eastern stories such as Enuma Elish and Atrahasis. Where those myths picture humans as slaves made to feed the gods, Genesis presents one God who speaks the world into order and makes humanity in his image to rule and care for it as his representatives (Gen 1:26–28).

The ancestral stories reflect 2nd-millennium customs (household gods, covenant meals, inheritance practices). They end with Jacob's family in Egypt, setting up the exodus.

blocks.subject: entry:book/gen
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Genesis opens with a Father who makes a world for fellowship: he walks in the garden and calls, "Where art thou?" (Gen 3:9). Sin is first a broken relationship, hiding from a Father who comes looking.

The promise that the woman's seed will crush the serpent (Gen 3:15) is the first note of Christus Victor: the story will end with the enemy defeated, not with God appeased. Irenaeus read Christ as the new Adam who goes back over the ground Adam lost and *recapitulates* it, healing humanity from within.

Abraham's call is about blessing the nations (Gen 12:3), which Paul calls "the gospel preached before" (Gal 3:8). Isaac on the mountain (Gen 22) points to a Father who provides the lamb himself. Joseph, rejected by his brothers and raised to save them, shows how God turns evil into rescue (Gen 50:20), the pattern of the cross.

blocks.subject: entry:book/gen
blocks.title: Who wrote the Torah?
blocks.body:
Jewish and Christian tradition holds that Moses wrote the five books of the Torah, and the books themselves say Moses wrote down laws, a travel log and a song (Exod 24:4; Num 33:2; Deut 31:9, 22). Conservative scholars defend a substantially Mosaic Torah with later updating, such as the notice of Moses' death (Deu 34) and older place names explained for later readers.

Most critical scholars since the 19th century see the Torah as compiled from several sources or traditions over centuries. The classic form (the Documentary Hypothesis: J, E, D, P) has been heavily revised, and many now prefer models of fragments and supplements edited in the exile or Persian period.

What is not in dispute: the Torah preserves very old material, and it reached its final shape well before the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Septuagint translation (3rd century BC) were made.

blocks.subject: entry:book/gen
blocks.title: Irenaeus: Christ recapitulates Adam
blocks.body: Irenaeus taught that the Son, becoming human, "summed up" (recapitulated) the long line of humanity in himself, so that what we lost in Adam, being in the image and likeness of God, we might recover in Christ. He set Adam against Christ and Eve against Mary as matched pairs in the story of rescue.

blocks.subject: entry:book/exo
blocks.body:
Exodus begins with Israel enslaved under an unnamed Pharaoh and ends with God's glory filling the tabernacle (Exod 40:34). In between, God reveals his name (Exod 3:14), defeats the gods of Egypt through the plagues (Exod 12:12), brings Israel through the sea, gives the Ten Words at Sinai and makes covenant with the people.

The book is as much about presence as freedom: half of it concerns the tabernacle, a portable sanctuary so that God can "dwell among them" (Exod 25:8). After the golden calf, God's self-description, "merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth" (Exod 34:6), becomes Israel's most quoted confession about God.

blocks.subject: entry:book/exo
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
God's first message to Pharaoh is a family claim: "Israel is my son, even my firstborn: let my son go" (Exod 4:22–23). The exodus is a Father rescuing a son, not a court verdict. Jesus relives that story: he is called out of Egypt (Matt 2:15), tested in the wilderness and faithful where Israel failed.

The Passover lamb shields the household and marks the night of liberation; Paul calls Christ "our passover" (1 Cor 5:7). The plagues are judgments on Egypt's gods, a picture of Christ disarming the powers (Col 2:15). The tabernacle, where God pitches his tent among his people, is fulfilled when "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt [tabernacled] among us" (John 1:14), and Moses' request to see God's glory is answered in the face of Jesus (2 Cor 4:6).

blocks.subject: entry:book/exo
blocks.title: When was the exodus?
blocks.body:
**Early date (c. 1446 BC):** 1 Kgs 6:1 places the exodus 480 years before Solomon's fourth year (c. 966 BC). Judg 11:26 (300 years in the land by Jephthah's time) fits this.

**Late date (c. 1270–1250 BC):** Exod 1:11 names the store city Raamses, linked to Pharaoh Ramesses II; the 480 years may be a symbolic 12 generations of 40 years. The Merneptah Stele (c. 1208 BC) names Israel as a people in Canaan by the late 13th century.

**Minimalist and critical views:** some scholars see the exodus as a later national memory with a small historical core, or none. Archaeology has not found direct evidence of a large migration, which is how both camps argue from silence.

blocks.subject: entry:book/lev
blocks.body:
Leviticus continues straight from Exodus: God now dwells in the tabernacle, so how can Israel live near him? The answer is a set of offerings, a priesthood, purity laws, a calendar of feasts and the Holiness Code (Lev 17–26), with its refrain "Ye shall be holy: for I the LORD your God am holy" (Lev 19:2).

The Hebrew word for offering, *qorban*, comes from a root meaning "to come near". Most offerings were meals or gifts shared at God's table, not only sin offerings. The Day of Atonement (Lev 16) cleansed the sanctuary and the people so God could keep living among them.

The book also contains the command quoted by Jesus as the second great commandment, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself" (Lev 19:18), and the Jubilee release of debts and land (Lev 25).

blocks.subject: entry:book/lev
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Leviticus is about nearness. The offerings are ways of coming close to a God who wants to live with his people, and the purity laws teach that death and decay cannot share space with the Living One.

In Jesus that movement is reversed: instead of uncleanness spreading to the holy, his holiness spreads to the unclean. He touches the leper (Mark 1:41) and the bleeding woman is healed when she touches him (Mark 5:25–34). Hebrews reads the Day of Atonement as Christ entering the true sanctuary with his own blood (Heb 9:11–14): the blood is life given (Lev 17:11) to cleanse and restore communion, not a payment to placate an angry deity.

Jesus announces "the acceptable year of the Lord" (Luke 4:19), the Jubilee language of release: debts cancelled, land restored, captives set free.

blocks.subject: entry:book/num
blocks.body:
Numbers takes its English name from two censuses (Num 1 and Num 26). Its Hebrew name, *Bemidbar*, means "in the wilderness", which is the real subject. The first generation leaves Sinai, refuses to enter Canaan after the spies' report (Num 14) and dies in the desert. Their children are counted at the end and prepare to cross the Jordan.

Along the way come the bronze serpent (Num 21), the priestly blessing (Num 6:24–26) and the strange story of Balaam, a foreign seer hired to curse Israel who can only bless (Num 22–24).

blocks.subject: entry:book/num
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The priestly blessing, "The LORD make his face shine upon thee" (Num 6:25), is the Father's desire for his people, and it is fulfilled in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6).

Jesus applies the bronze serpent to himself: "as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up" (John 3:14). The people look at the very thing that was killing them and live; at the cross, death is lifted up and defeated in plain view.

Balaam's oracle of "a Star out of Jacob" (Num 24:17) was read as messianic in Second Temple Judaism. Paul reads the rock that followed Israel as Christ (1 Cor 10:4): God did not abandon his grumbling children but travelled with them and fed them.

blocks.subject: entry:book/deu
blocks.body:
Deuteronomy ("second law") is a series of speeches by Moses to the generation about to enter Canaan. It retells the journey, repeats the Ten Words, and lays out laws for life in the land, ending with blessings, curses, a song and Moses' death on Mount Nebo.

Its form resembles ancient treaties between a great king and a vassal: history, stipulations, witnesses, blessings and curses. Its heart is the Shema: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD: and thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart" (Deut 6:4–5). It repeatedly commands care for the widow, the orphan and the stranger.

Jesus quoted Deuteronomy all three times when tempted in the wilderness (Matt 4:1–11).

blocks.subject: entry:book/deu
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Deuteronomy is a love story told as a covenant. God does not choose Israel because it is impressive but "because the LORD loved you" (Deut 7:8), and he carries them "as a man doth bear his son" (Deut 1:31).

Jesus calls the Shema the first commandment (Mark 12:29–30): the law is fulfilled in love. He is the prophet "like unto" Moses whom God promised to raise (Deut 18:15; Acts 3:22), and as the faithful Son he answers every temptation from Deuteronomy, succeeding where Israel failed.

Deuteronomy already looks past Israel's failure to a day when "the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart" (Deut 30:6). Paul hears in Deut 30:12–14 the nearness of Christ himself (Rom 10:6–8). The curses of the covenant are not the last word: they lead to exile and return, which the gospels present as fulfilled in Jesus.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jos
blocks.body:
Joshua tells how Israel crossed the Jordan, took Jericho and fought campaigns in the south and north, then divided the land among the tribes. It closes with a covenant renewal at Shechem: "choose you this day whom ye will serve" (Josh 24:15).

The book shows its own complexity. Sweeping claims of total conquest (Josh 11:23) stand beside admissions that much land remained (Josh 13:1) and that Canaanites still lived among Israel (Josh 15:63). Rahab, a Canaanite, is saved and joins Israel, while Achan, an Israelite, is judged. Ancient conquest accounts commonly used hyperbolic language, which helps explain the tension.

Archaeologists debate how the conquest relates to the evidence; many see a more gradual settlement.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jos
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
"Joshua" and "Jesus" are the same name (Hebrew *Yehoshua*, Greek *Iēsous*): "the LORD saves". Hebrews notes that Joshua did not give the final rest (Heb 4:8); the true rest is in the Son.

Reading Joshua through Jesus matters most at the hardest point: the violence. Jesus is perfect theology, so the conquest is not the clearest picture of the Father. The Commander of the LORD's army refuses to be on anyone's side (Josh 5:13–14), and Rahab's rescue shows the door was open to Canaanites who turned to Israel's God. Jesus conquers by laying down his life, and the "land" he gives is the whole earth reclaimed for the kingdom (Matt 5:5; Rom 4:13), taken not with the sword but by the gospel.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jos
blocks.title: Conquest and archaeology
blocks.body:
Scholars disagree on how the conquest happened and when the book was written.

- **Traditional:** a real military entry around 1400 BC (early exodus) or 1230 BC (late exodus), recorded close to the events.
- **Majority critical:** Joshua is part of a Deuteronomistic History edited in the 7th–6th centuries BC from older traditions; the settlement was largely gradual or internal.
- **Archaeology:** Jericho's walls and the date of their fall are debated; Hazor shows a major destruction in the 13th century BC; Ai is hard to match with any site's occupation history.

The book's own language is partly hyperbolic, which ancient readers would have recognised.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jdg
blocks.body:
Judges follows a repeating pattern: Israel serves other gods, falls under an oppressor, cries out, and God raises a "judge" (deliverer) to rescue them (Judg 2:11–19). Each cycle gets worse. The judges themselves become more compromised, from Othniel and Deborah to Gideon's ephod, Jephthah's vow and Samson's appetites.

The last chapters (Jdg 17–21) show a society in moral free fall, framed by the refrain "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25).

blocks.subject: entry:book/jdg
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Judges shows a Father who keeps answering his children's cry even when they keep running away: "his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel" (Judg 10:16). Mercy is not earned by reform; God rescues again and again.

Each judge is a partial deliverer, and each flaw makes the reader long for a true one. Samson dies with arms stretched out, defeating the enemy in his death (Judg 16:30), a broken echo of the cross where Christ triumphs over the powers. The cry for a king (Judg 21:25) is answered not finally by David but by the Son who rules with justice and peace, and who does what is right in the Father's eyes rather than his own (John 5:19).

blocks.subject: entry:book/jdg
blocks.title: Prophetic history or Deuteronomistic History?
blocks.body:
**Traditional view:** Jewish tradition (b. Bava Batra 14b–15a) assigns these books to prophets close to the events: Joshua, Samuel, Nathan and Gad, and Jeremiah. The books themselves cite earlier written sources, such as "the book of Jasher" (Josh 10:13; 2 Sam 1:18) and "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel" (1 Kgs 14:19).

**Majority critical view:** Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings form a "Deuteronomistic History", one connected work judging Israel's past by the standards of Deuteronomy. A first edition is often placed under Josiah (late 7th century BC) and a final edition in the exile, after the last event recorded (562 BC, 2 Kgs 25:27).

**Common ground:** both views accept that the books draw on older records; the disagreement is about who shaped them and when.

blocks.subject: entry:book/rut
blocks.body:
Ruth is set in the time of the judges but reads very differently: no battles, only ordinary people acting with *hesed*, loyal covenant love. Naomi loses her husband and sons in Moab and returns to Bethlehem with her Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth, who pledges, "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God" (Ruth 1:16).

Boaz, a relative, protects Ruth as she gleans (a practice from Lev 19:9–10) and finally acts as *go'el*, kinsman-redeemer, buying back the family land and marrying her (Rut 4). Their son Obed is David's grandfather. In Jewish practice Ruth is read at Shavuot (Pentecost).

blocks.subject: entry:book/rut
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The *go'el* is family, not a stranger: a redeemer is the relative who restores what was lost, buys back land and keeps a family name alive. That is the shape of redemption in Christ, who "is not ashamed to call them brethren" (Heb 2:11). Redemption here is restoration into a family, not a transaction for its own sake.

Ruth the Moabite, legally excluded (Deut 23:3), is brought into Israel's story and into the line of the Messiah (Matt 1:5). The gospel's welcome of outsiders is not a later idea; it is in David's own family tree.

blocks.subject: entry:book/rut
blocks.title: Early or late?
blocks.body: Most scholars date Ruth to the monarchy because its Hebrew is classical and its genealogy ends with David (Ruth 4:17–22). A minority date it after the exile and read it as a quiet protest against the strict policy on foreign wives in Ezr 9–10 and Neh 13: a Moabite woman becomes David's great-grandmother. Both readings agree on the book's point: covenant loyalty, not ancestry, marks the people of God.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1sa
blocks.body:
1 Samuel (one book with 2 Samuel in the Hebrew Bible) covers the move from the judges to kingship. Hannah's prayer is answered with Samuel, the last judge and a prophet. The ark is captured by the Philistines and returned. Israel asks for a king "like all the nations" (1 Sam 8:5), and Samuel warns what kings take.

Saul begins well but disobeys and is rejected. God sends Samuel to anoint David, the youngest son, because "the LORD looketh on the heart" (1 Sam 16:7). Most of the book follows David's rise and his refusal to harm Saul, "the LORD's anointed", even when he could.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1sa
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Hannah's song (1 Sam 2:1–10), where God lifts the poor from the dust, is the template for Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46–55). It is also the first place in Scripture where the king is called God's "anointed", *messiah* (1 Sam 2:10).

David, overlooked by his own family and anointed in secret, is the shepherd-king who defeats the giant on behalf of a frightened people. Jesus is the Son of David who defeats the enemy not with a sling but with his own death and resurrection, and does it for us, as our representative. David's refusal to seize the throne by force (1Sa 24; 26) foreshadows a Messiah who will not grasp power (Phil 2:6).

blocks.subject: entry:book/2sa
blocks.body:
2 Samuel tells David's reign. He becomes king of Judah at Hebron, then of all Israel, captures Jerusalem and brings the ark there. In 2Sa 7 God promises that David's offspring will build a house for his name and that "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (2 Sam 7:14), with a throne established for ever.

Then the story turns. David takes Bathsheba and arranges Uriah's death (2Sa 11). Nathan confronts him, David repents (Psa 51), but violence spreads through his family: Amnon, Absalom's revolt and civil war.

David's kindness to Mephibosheth, Saul's lame grandson, who eats at the king's table "as one of the king's sons" (2 Sam 9:11), is one of the book's quiet high points.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2sa
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The Davidic covenant is a Father–Son covenant: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (2 Sam 7:14). Hebrews applies it to Jesus (Heb 1:5), and through him to all who share his sonship (2 Cor 6:18).

Mephibosheth, unable to come to the king and brought to his table as a son, is a picture of grace and adoption. David's failures show that the promised everlasting king had to be more than David. Jesus, Son of David, takes the throne at his resurrection and ascension (Acts 2:30–36), and his kingdom now grows until it fills the earth.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1ki
blocks.body:
1 Kings opens with Solomon's accession, his request for wisdom and the building of the temple, dedicated with a prayer that even foreigners would be heard (1 Kgs 8:41–43). Solomon's many foreign wives turn his heart to other gods, and after his death the kingdom splits (c. 930 BC): Israel in the north under Jeroboam, Judah in the south under Rehoboam.

Every king is assessed by one question: did he do right in the eyes of the LORD? The second half focuses on Elijah, who confronts Ahab and Jezebel, defeats Baal's prophets on Mount Carmel (1Ki 18) and hears God in "a still small voice" (1 Kgs 19:12).

blocks.subject: entry:book/1ki
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Solomon's temple is where heaven and earth meet. Jesus says "in this place is one greater than the temple" (Matt 12:6) and speaks of his body as the temple (John 2:19–21). In him, God's dwelling is no longer a building in one city but a person, and then a people (Eph 2:21–22).

Solomon asked for wisdom; Jesus is the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24), and "a greater than Solomon is here" (Matt 12:42). Elijah's showdown at Carmel ends with fire falling on the sacrifice; the God who answers by fire answered at Pentecost with tongues of fire. God whispering to the exhausted prophet shows the Father's tenderness, food and sleep before instructions (1 Kgs 19:5–8).

blocks.subject: entry:book/1ki
blocks.title: Prophetic history or Deuteronomistic History?
blocks.body:
**Traditional view:** Jewish tradition (b. Bava Batra 14b–15a) assigns these books to prophets close to the events: Joshua, Samuel, Nathan and Gad, and Jeremiah. The books themselves cite earlier written sources, such as "the book of Jasher" (Josh 10:13; 2 Sam 1:18) and "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel" (1 Kgs 14:19).

**Majority critical view:** Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings form a "Deuteronomistic History", one connected work judging Israel's past by the standards of Deuteronomy. A first edition is often placed under Josiah (late 7th century BC) and a final edition in the exile, after the last event recorded (562 BC, 2 Kgs 25:27).

**Common ground:** both views accept that the books draw on older records; the disagreement is about who shaped them and when.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2ki
blocks.body:
2 Kings continues the story. Elijah is taken up and Elisha performs many signs, including healing Naaman the Syrian (2Ki 5). The northern kingdom falls to Assyria in 722 BC, and the writer explains why at length (2Ki 17).

Judah survives longer. Hezekiah trusts God when Sennacherib besieges Jerusalem (701 BC, also recorded in Assyrian annals), and Josiah reforms worship after the "book of the law" is found (2Ki 22–23). But Babylon takes Jerusalem in 586 BC and burns the temple. The book ends with King Jehoiachin released from prison and eating at the Babylonian king's table (2 Kgs 25:27–30), a small sign that David's line survives.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2ki
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Elisha's ministry looks like a preview of Jesus: multiplying bread (2 Kgs 4:42–44), raising a widow's son, cleansing a foreign leper. Jesus himself points to Naaman to show that God's grace reaches beyond Israel (Luke 4:27).

The book ends in exile, the curse of Deuteronomy fulfilled, yet with a son of David alive and eating at a king's table. The gospels present Jesus as the end of exile: the true King who goes into the place of death and comes out, bringing his people home to the Father.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2ki
blocks.title: Prophetic history or Deuteronomistic History?
