The books themselves cite earlier written sources, such as "the book of Jasher" (Josh 10:13; 2 Sam 1:18) and "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel" (1 Kgs 14:19).

**Majority critical view:** Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings form a "Deuteronomistic History", one connected work judging Israel's past by the standards of Deuteronomy. A first edition is often placed under Josiah (late 7th century BC) and a final edition in the exile, after the last event recorded (562 BC, 2 Kgs 25:27).

**Common ground:** both views accept that the books draw on older records; the disagreement is about who shaped them and when.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1ch
blocks.body:
Chronicles (one book in the Hebrew Bible, and its last book) retells Israel's story for the community back from exile. It opens with nine chapters of genealogies from Adam, assuring the returnees that they belong to a long story.

1 Chronicles focuses on David, but a different David from Samuel's: the Bathsheba affair is not retold. Instead David brings the ark to Jerusalem, organises Levites and musicians, and prepares materials for the temple. The writer uses Samuel and Kings as sources and cites others.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1ch
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The genealogies start with Adam, not Abraham: Israel's story is humanity's story. Luke's genealogy of Jesus does the same, tracing him back to "Adam, which was the son of God" (Luke 3:38). Jesus is the new head of the human family.

The Chronicler's David is a worship leader whose kingdom centres on God's presence and praise. The promise "I will be his father, and he shall be my son" (1 Chr 17:13) points to Jesus, the Son in whom the kingdom becomes a house of prayer for all nations.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2ch
blocks.body:
2 Chronicles follows Judah's kings from Solomon to the exile, largely ignoring the northern kingdom. Its key verse is God's promise: "If my people... shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face... then will I hear from heaven" (2 Chr 7:14).

The Chronicler stresses that repentance changes things. Even Manasseh, the worst king in Kings, repents in Babylon and is restored (2 Chr 33:12–13). The book, and the Hebrew Bible, ends with Cyrus' decree: "Who is there among you... let him go up" (2 Chr 36:23).

blocks.subject: entry:book/2ch
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Chronicles shows a God who keeps restoring those who turn back, even Manasseh. That is the Father of the prodigal son, running to meet the returning child (Luke 15:20).

The Hebrew Bible ends with an open invitation to "go up" to Jerusalem and rebuild God's house. The New Testament picks up the thread: Jesus goes up to Jerusalem, rebuilds the temple in three days in his body (John 2:19), and sends his people to all nations.

blocks.subject: entry:book/ezr
blocks.body:
Ezra (one book with Nehemiah in the Hebrew Bible) covers two waves of return. In 538 BC Cyrus of Persia lets exiles go home; under Zerubbabel and Jeshua they rebuild the altar and, after a long delay, finish the temple in 516/515 BC with encouragement from Haggai and Zechariah.

Decades later Ezra, "a ready scribe in the law of Moses" (Ezra 7:6), arrives with royal backing. The book ends with a painful crisis over marriages to foreign wives. Part of the book is in Aramaic, the official language of the Persian empire.

blocks.subject: entry:book/ezr
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Ezra shows God keeping his word "by the mouth of Jeremiah" (Ezra 1:1) and moving a pagan emperor's heart. The return is real but partial: older people weep because the new temple is smaller than the first (Ezra 3:12), and the people are still "servants" in their own land (Neh 9:36).

The gospels present Jesus as the full end of exile. He is the true temple, and he gathers not only Judah but people from every nation. The marriage crisis shows a community protecting its identity; in Christ identity is guarded by union with him, which opens the family to outsiders rather than closing it (Eph 2:14–19).

blocks.subject: entry:book/ezr
blocks.title: Did Ezra come before Nehemiah?
blocks.body:
The books place Ezra's arrival in "the seventh year of Artaxerxes" (Ezra 7:7) and Nehemiah's in the twentieth (Neh 2:1). If both kings are Artaxerxes I, Ezra came in 458 BC and Nehemiah in 445 BC, which is the traditional order and still the majority view.

Some scholars argue Ezra came under Artaxerxes II (398 BC), after Nehemiah, because Ezra seems to find a rebuilt, populated Jerusalem and the two men rarely appear together. Others propose emending the text to "thirty-seventh year" (c. 428 BC). These alternatives are minority positions.

blocks.subject: entry:book/neh
blocks.body:
Nehemiah, cupbearer to Artaxerxes I, hears that Jerusalem's walls lie in ruins. He prays, asks the king for leave, and in 445 BC returns as governor. Despite threats from Sanballat and Tobiah, the walls are finished in 52 days (Neh 6:15).

In Neh 8 Ezra reads the law aloud from morning to midday while Levites explain it, and the people weep. They are told: "the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Neh 8:10). A long prayer of confession (Neh 9) retells Israel's history of God's mercy. The book ends with Nehemiah confronting abuses after a second visit.

blocks.subject: entry:book/neh
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The great prayer of Neh 9 is a confession of a Father's patience: "thou art a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and forsookest them not" (Neh 9:17).

Rebuilt walls and a renewed covenant are good but fragile; by Neh 13 the same problems are back. That points beyond reform to new birth. Jesus builds a city not with stones but with people, "lively stones" (1 Pet 2:5), and gives the Spirit to write the law on hearts, which Ezra's reading could not do.

blocks.subject: entry:book/est
blocks.body:
Esther is set in the Persian court of Ahasuerus (Xerxes I). Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, becomes queen. When the official Haman plots to destroy all Jews, Mordecai urges her: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esth 4:14). She goes to the king uninvited, at risk of death, and the plot is reversed: Haman hangs on the gallows he built.

The festival of Purim celebrates this deliverance. God is never mentioned in the Hebrew text, and Esther was the one Hebrew Bible book not found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. The Greek version adds prayers and mentions of God (part of the deuterocanon).

blocks.subject: entry:book/est
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
God's name is hidden, but his care is not: chance, sleepless nights and timing all bend toward rescue. The Father is often most present where he is least visible.

Esther stands between the king and her people, saying "if I perish, I perish" (Esth 4:16). Jesus goes further: he does not just risk death but enters it to bring his people out. The great reversal of Esther, the gallows turned against the one who built it, is the shape of the cross, where the powers that crucified Christ were themselves disarmed (Col 2:15).

blocks.subject: entry:book/est
blocks.title: History or historical novella?
blocks.body:
Esther's Persian detail is accurate: the palace at Susa, the postal system, the king's banquets and Xerxes' character fit what Greek historians report about the Persian court. Many conservative scholars read it as history.

Many critical scholars read it as a historical novella: the Greek historians name Xerxes' queen as Amestris, not Vashti or Esther, and the irrevocable "laws of the Medes and Persians" and the scale of events are hard to confirm. Some propose that Esther was a lesser wife, or that names have been changed. The disagreement concerns genre, not the book's message of providence and courage.

blocks.subject: entry:book/job
blocks.body:
Job opens in prose: a blameless man loses his children, wealth and health after the accuser ("the satan") challenges whether Job serves God for nothing. Then comes long poetry. Three friends argue that suffering is always punishment; Job insists he is innocent and calls for a hearing with God. A younger man, Elihu, speaks. Finally the LORD answers from a whirlwind with questions about creation that put Job's suffering in a vast frame.

God then says the friends "have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath" (Job 42:7). Job's raw protest is honoured over their tidy theology. His fortunes are restored.

blocks.subject: entry:book/job
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The friends' theology is "you suffer because you sinned", and God rejects it. Jesus does too (John 9:2–3; Luke 13:1–5). The Father is not the author of every calamity; the accuser is.

Job longs for "a daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both" (Job 9:33) and declares "I know that my redeemer liveth" (Job 19:25). In Jesus that longing is met: God himself, in the Son, steps into undeserved suffering, stands with the sufferer and opens the way through death. The cross is God's answer to Job, not an explanation of pain but God sharing it and defeating it.

blocks.subject: entry:book/job
blocks.title: When was Job written?
blocks.body:
The setting is patriarchal: wealth counted in herds, Job acting as priest for his family, no reference to Israel's law or history. Some take this as evidence of very early composition.

Most scholars distinguish setting from writing. The polished Hebrew poetry, Aramaic touches and the debate with the idea that suffering always proves guilt suggest the monarchy or the exile, when Israel was asking why the righteous suffer. A minority hold that an old prose folktale was later framed around new poetry. The book's date is uncertain and its message does not depend on it.

blocks.subject: entry:book/psa
blocks.body:
The Psalms are 150 poems in five books, each ending with a doxology (Ps 41:13; 72:19; 89:52; 106:48; 150). Psa 1–2 introduce the collection: the person who delights in God's instruction, and God's anointed king.

The main types are hymns of praise, laments (the largest group), thanksgivings, royal psalms and wisdom psalms. Lament psalms let worshippers complain, protest and question God, and nearly all of them turn to trust. The refrain "his mercy endureth for ever" (*hesed*) runs through the collection (Psa 136).

The Psalms were Jesus' prayer book, and they are the Old Testament book most quoted in the New Testament.

blocks.subject: entry:book/psa
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The Psalms are the prayers Jesus prayed. On the cross he prays Ps 22:1, "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?", a psalm that ends in vindication and praise among the nations (Ps 22:27). His last words come from Ps 31:5: "into thine hand I commit my spirit", spoken to his Father.

Psa 2 announces the Son: "Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee" (Ps 2:7), applied to Jesus' resurrection (Acts 13:33). Psa 110, the Old Testament text most quoted in the New, shows the Son seated at the Father's right hand "until I make thine enemies thy footstool": the risen Christ reigns now while his enemies are progressively subdued (1 Cor 15:25). The kingdom psalms (Psa 72; 96–99) picture a king whose rule brings justice to the poor and fills the earth.

blocks.subject: entry:book/pro
blocks.body:
Proverbs is a collection of collections. Chapters 1–9 are longer poems in which a father urges his son to choose Lady Wisdom over Folly. Wisdom is pictured as present with God at creation, "rejoicing always before him" (Prov 8:30). Chapters 10–29 gather short two-line sayings about speech, work, money, friendship and justice. The book ends with Agur's riddles, Lemuel's mother's advice and an acrostic poem praising "a virtuous woman" (Prov 31:10–31).

A section (Prov 22:17–24:22) closely parallels the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, showing Israel's sages learning from neighbours. Proverbs are generalisations about how life usually goes, not guarantees.

blocks.subject: entry:book/pro
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The book is framed as a father teaching a son: "My son, hear the instruction of thy father" (Prov 1:8). Wisdom is relational, passed on in a family.

Lady Wisdom, beside God at creation and delighting in humanity (Prov 8:22–31), is the background for the New Testament's description of Christ as the one through whom all things were made (John 1:1–3; Col 1:15–17). Paul calls Christ "the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24), and "in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom" (Col 2:3). Wisdom in Proverbs is not rule-keeping; it is life shaped by friendship with the God who made the world.

blocks.subject: entry:book/ecc
blocks.body:
Ecclesiastes is narrated by Qoheleth, "the Preacher" or "gatherer". His keyword *hevel* ("vanity" in the KJV) means vapour or breath: life is fleeting and cannot be grasped. He tests pleasure, work, wealth and wisdom and finds that death levels everyone.

Yet seven times he commends joy: eating, drinking and enjoying work and love as gifts from God (Eccl 2:24; 9:7–9). The epilogue sums up: "Fear God, and keep his commandments" (Eccl 12:13). The book is read at the feast of Tabernacles in Jewish practice.

blocks.subject: entry:book/ecc
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Qoheleth names honestly what life "under the sun" looks like without resurrection: everything slips through the fingers. Paul echoes him when he says creation was "made subject to vanity" (Rom 8:20, the same Greek word the Septuagint uses for *hevel*) and adds what Qoheleth could not see: it was subjected "in hope".

In Jesus, the one who entered our fleeting life and death, the vapour is not the last word. Because of the resurrection our labour "is not in vain in the Lord" (1 Cor 15:58). The Preacher's call to receive food, work and love as gifts is the life of a child who trusts the Father.

blocks.subject: entry:book/ecc
blocks.title: Solomon or Qoheleth?
blocks.body:
The book never names Solomon; it calls its speaker "the son of David, king in Jerusalem" (Eccl 1:1). Jewish and Christian tradition identified him with Solomon, and some conservative scholars still do.

Most scholars, including many evangelicals, see the Solomonic voice as a literary persona used in Ecc 1–2 and then dropped. They point to late Hebrew, Persian loanwords and a narrator who speaks about Qoheleth in the third person (Eccl 12:9–10). On this view the book is a later sage's reflection in the tradition of Solomon's wisdom.

blocks.subject: entry:book/sng
blocks.body:
The Song of Songs is a set of love poems in which a woman and her beloved speak to each other, with a chorus of the "daughters of Jerusalem". The woman speaks more than the man. The imagery is lush: gardens, vineyards, spices, gazelles. Their love is mutual: "My beloved is mine, and I am his" (Song 2:16).

The book never mentions God directly (unless in Song 8:6, "a most vehement flame", Hebrew *shalhebetyah*, ending with a short form of the divine name). Rabbinic debate over whether it belonged in Scripture is recorded in Mishnah Yadayim 3:5. Jews read it at Passover; Jewish and Christian interpreters long read it allegorically as God and Israel or Christ and the church.

blocks.subject: entry:book/sng
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The Song first honours human love as good: God made bodies, desire and delight, and called them very good.

Read through Jesus, it also gives language for the divine romance that runs through Scripture: God as husband to Israel (Hos 2:16–20), Christ as bridegroom (Mark 2:19), the church as bride (Eph 5:25–32; Rev 19:7). This is the relational heart of the gospel: God wants union, not just compliance. "I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me" (Song 7:10) reverses the curse of Gen 3:16, where desire became distorted. In Christ, love is "strong as death" (Song 8:6), and stronger.

blocks.subject: entry:book/sng
blocks.title: Debated at Yavneh
blocks.body: The Mishnah records a debate among rabbis about whether the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes "defile the hands", the rabbinic way of saying a book is sacred Scripture. Rabbi Akiva defended the Song strongly. The discussion shows that the Song's place was questioned but upheld.

blocks.subject: entry:book/isa
blocks.body:
Isaiah's call comes "in the year that king Uzziah died" (c. 740 BC), when he sees the LORD enthroned and hears "Holy, holy, holy" (Isa 6). Chapters 1–39 address Judah during the Assyrian crisis: Ahaz is offered the sign of Immanuel (Isa 7:14), and Hezekiah is delivered from Sennacherib (Isa 36–37).

From chapter 40 the horizon is the Babylonian exile: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people" (Isa 40:1). God promises a new exodus, names Cyrus as his instrument and introduces the Servant of the LORD, who suffers for others (Isa 52:13–53:12). The book ends with new heavens and a new earth (Isa 65:17).

The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (c. 2nd century BC) contains all 66 chapters and is one of the oldest biblical manuscripts.

blocks.subject: entry:book/isa
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus begins his ministry by reading Isa 61:1–2: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me... to preach the gospel to the poor... to set at liberty them that are bruised" (Luke 4:18–19). He stops before "the day of vengeance": his mission is release.

Isaiah sees the child called "Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace", whose government and peace grow without end (Isa 9:6–7), a promise of a kingdom that increases through history. The Servant of Isa 53 bears our griefs and sicknesses (applied to healing in Matt 8:17) and makes many righteous. The New Testament reads this as solidarity and victory: the Servant enters our condition, is crushed by human violence, and is vindicated, and "the pleasure of the LORD shall prosper in his hand" (Isa 53:10).

The mountain of the LORD where swords become ploughshares (Isa 2:2–4) and the earth full of the knowledge of the LORD (Isa 11:9) are the long hope of the gospel's spread.

blocks.subject: entry:book/isa
blocks.title: One Isaiah or several?
blocks.body:
**Unity view:** Isaiah of Jerusalem wrote the whole book in the 8th century BC, foreseeing the exile and naming Cyrus about 150 years in advance. Supporters stress the title "the Holy One of Israel", which appears throughout both halves and rarely elsewhere, and the New Testament's practice of quoting both halves as "Isaiah" (John 12:38–41). The Great Isaiah Scroll shows no break after chapter 39.

**Multiple-author view (majority):** chapters 40–66 address people already in exile, call Cyrus by name as a present figure and differ in style. Many scholars see a "school" of Isaiah's disciples (Isa 8:16) extending his message to new situations. Some evangelical scholars hold a version of this view.

New Testament citation of "Isaiah" can be read as naming the scroll rather than settling authorship; scholars differ on this too.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jer
blocks.body:
Jeremiah was called as a young man (Jer 1:6) and preached from about 627 BC through the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, dying in Egypt. He attacked trust in the temple as a lucky charm (Jer 7), was beaten, imprisoned and thrown into a cistern, and bought a field during the siege as a sign that the land had a future (Jer 32).

His book is not in chronological order. It includes his raw personal laments (Jer 11–20), symbolic acts and the Book of Consolation (Jer 30–33). The Greek Septuagint version is shorter than the Hebrew and orders the oracles against the nations differently; both forms were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jer
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Jeremiah's heartbreak reveals a heartbroken God: "Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child?... my bowels are troubled for him" (Jer 31:20). God speaks as a Father longing for a runaway son, and as a husband grieving a faithless bride (Jer 3).

The new covenant (Jer 31:31–34) is relational at its core: "I will put my law in their inward parts... and they shall all know me." Jesus inaugurates it at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews quotes it at length (Heb 8:8–12). Forgiveness here is the ground of a restored relationship. Jesus, like Jeremiah, weeps over Jerusalem and warns of its coming destruction (Luke 19:41–44), fulfilled in AD 70.

blocks.subject: entry:book/lam
blocks.body:
Lamentations is five poems mourning the fall of Jerusalem. The first four are acrostics, each verse or group of verses beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, a way of grieving "from A to Z". Chapter 3, at the centre, triples the acrostic and holds the book's best-known lines: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning" (Lam 3:22–23).

Jews read Lamentations on Tisha b'Av, the fast that remembers the destruction of both temples.

blocks.subject: entry:book/lam
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Lamentations gives God's people permission to grieve honestly before him. Its central confession, "the Lord will not cast off for ever... he doth not afflict willingly" (Lam 3:31–33), reveals a Father whose heart is not in punishment.

Jesus enters this kind of grief. He weeps over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41) and on the cross takes up the cry of abandonment. Lam 1:12, "Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by?", has long been read in Holy Week of Christ. The God who seemed absent in Lamentations is, in Jesus, present in the ruins.

blocks.subject: entry:book/ezk
blocks.body:
Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon in 597 BC. His book opens with a staggering vision of God's glory on a chariot-throne by the river Chebar (Ezk 1): God is not confined to Jerusalem. Ezekiel acts out strange signs and, in a vision, watches the glory leave the temple (Ezk 10–11) before Babylon destroys it.

After the fall, the message turns to hope: God himself will shepherd his scattered sheep (Ezk 34), give a new heart and his Spirit (Ezek 36:26–27), and raise a valley of dry bones (Ezk 37). The book ends with a vision of a new temple, a river flowing out to heal the Dead Sea (Ezk 47) and a city named "The LORD is there" (Ezek 48:35).

blocks.subject: entry:book/ezk
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
God says, "I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out" (Ezek 34:11). Jesus answers: "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11). The Father does not send a hired hand; he comes himself.

The new heart and Spirit of Ezk 36 is the new birth Jesus speaks of to Nicodemus, "born of water and of the Spirit" (John 3:5), a teacher of Israel expected to know Ezekiel. The river flowing from the temple becomes Jesus' promise of rivers of living water flowing from within believers (John 7:38) and the river of life in Rev 22:1–2. The returning glory is seen in Jesus (John 1:14) and the city "The LORD is there" is the New Jerusalem where God dwells with his people.

Partial-preterist and postmillennial readers note that the healing river grows deeper as it flows (Ezek 47:3–5): a picture of the kingdom's gradual, world-healing growth.

blocks.subject: entry:book/dan
blocks.body:
Daniel has two halves. Chapters 1–6 are court stories: Daniel and his friends refuse the king's food, survive the furnace and the lions' den, and see proud kings humbled. Chapters 7–12 are visions of beasts, empires and a coming kingdom. The book is bilingual: Dan 2:4–7:28 is in Aramaic, the rest in Hebrew.

In Dan 2 a stone "cut out without hands" strikes a statue of four kingdoms and "became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth" (Dan 2:35). In Dan 7 "one like the Son of man" comes to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom (Dan 7:13–14). Dan 9 gives seventy "weeks" until an anointed one is cut off, and Dan 12:2 contains the Old Testament's clearest statement of bodily resurrection.

blocks.subject: entry:book/dan
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
"Son of Man" is Jesus' favourite title for himself, taken from Dan 7. At his trial he tells the high priest, "ye shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven" (Mark 14:62). In Daniel the Son of Man comes *to* the Ancient of Days, upward, to receive a kingdom: fulfilled in Jesus' ascension and enthronement, and vindicated in AD 70, which those standing there would see.

The stone that becomes a mountain filling the earth is the kingdom Jesus established in the days of the fourth empire, Rome (Dan 2:44). It starts small and grows until it fills everything: Jesus' own parables of the mustard seed and leaven say the same (Matt 13:31–33). This is the backbone of a hopeful, postmillennial reading: the kingdom is already given and is growing now.

The fourth man in the furnace, "like the Son of God" (Dan 3:25), is a picture of the God who does not keep us from the fire but walks in it with us.

blocks.subject: entry:book/dan
blocks.title: Sixth century or second century BC?
blocks.body:
**Early date (minority):** the book presents Daniel as a 6th-century exile. Supporters argue that predictive prophecy is possible, that copies of Daniel at Qumran (some from the late 2nd century BC) and its acceptance as Scripture so soon after a supposed 165 BC origin are hard to explain, and that Jesus calls him "Daniel the prophet" (Matt 24:15). Many also read the fourth kingdom as Rome, which would place fulfilment after the Maccabean period.

**Maccabean date (majority):** Dan 11 tracks Hellenistic kings in remarkable detail up to Antiochus IV's desecration of the temple (167 BC) and then describes his end in a way that did not happen, suggesting a writer around 165 BC. Historical difficulties (e.g. "Darius the Mede", Belshazzar called king) and late language are also cited. On this view the fourth kingdom is Greece.

The ancient philosopher Porphyry already argued for a Maccabean date; Jerome answered him (see below). The question is tied to assumptions about prophecy as well as evidence.

blocks.subject: entry:book/dan
blocks.title: Jerome answers Porphyry
blocks.body: Jerome reports that the pagan critic Porphyry claimed Daniel was written not by Daniel but by someone living in Judea in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, who described past events as if predicting them. Jerome wrote his commentary partly to answer this and argued that the prophecies reach beyond Antiochus to Christ and the Antichrist.

blocks.subject: entry:book/hos
blocks.body:
Hosea preached in the northern kingdom in its final, chaotic decades. God tells him to marry Gomer, who is unfaithful; their children receive sign-names, "Not pitied" and "Not my people", and then are renamed "My people" (Hos 1–2). Hosea buys his wife back (Hos 3).

The charge against Israel is lack of "knowledge of God" (Hos 4:1), meaning intimate, covenant knowing, not information. God says, "I desired mercy [*hesed*], and not sacrifice" (Hos 6:6), a verse Jesus quotes twice (Matt 9:13; 12:7).

blocks.subject: entry:book/hos
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Hosea is perhaps the Old Testament's clearest window into the Father's heart: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt... I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms... How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?... mine heart is turned within me" (Hos 11:1–8). God's anger is the anger of wounded love, and love wins: "I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger".

Matthew applies "out of Egypt have I called my son" to Jesus (Matt 2:15): he is the faithful Son who relives Israel's story. Hosea buying back his wife is redemption as a husband restoring a marriage, and Paul uses "not my people... my people" for Gentiles brought into the family (Rom 9:25–26). "After two days will he revive us: in the third day he will raise us up" (Hos 6:2) is echoed in Jesus' third-day resurrection.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jol
blocks.body:
Joel begins with a real disaster: locusts have stripped the land. He calls the people to fast and return to God, "for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness" (Joel 2:13), echoing Exod 34:6.

God answers with promises of restored harvests ("I will restore to you the years that the locust hath eaten", Joel 2:25) and then: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy" (Joel 2:28). The book's date is uncertain, which is why it sits early in the Twelve but is often dated late.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jol
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
On the day of Pentecost Peter says, "this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16–21). The outpoured Spirit is the Spirit of sonship (Rom 8:15), crying "Abba, Father" in all who belong to Christ, without regard to age, gender or status.

Peter places the "last days" in his own generation, culminating in "the great and notable day of the Lord" with signs in heaven: language Old Testament prophets used for the fall of nations, fulfilled for Jerusalem in AD 70 (a partial-preterist reading). The call stands: "whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be saved" (Acts 2:21). The God who restores locust-eaten years is the Father who makes all things new.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jol
blocks.title: When did Joel prophesy?
blocks.body: Joel gives no king's name and no clear date. An **early date** (9th century BC, during the boy-king Joash) rests on the book's place among early prophets and the absence of a king. A **post-exilic date** (majority) rests on the standing temple with no mention of a king, the role of elders and priests, the mention of Greeks as slave-traders (Joel 3:6) and Joel's many echoes of other prophets. Some propose a date near the end of the monarchy. The message is not tied to the date.

blocks.subject: entry:book/amo
blocks.body:
Amos was not a professional prophet but "an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit" (Amos 7:14) from Judah, sent to Israel at the height of its wealth. He begins by condemning the nations around Israel, drawing applause, then turns on Israel itself for selling "the poor for a pair of shoes" (Amos 2:6).

God rejects worship that ignores justice: "let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream" (Amos 5:24). Israel expected the day of the LORD to be a victory; Amos says it will be darkness for them (Amos 5:18). The book ends with God raising up "the tabernacle of David that is fallen" (Amos 9:11).

blocks.subject: entry:book/amo
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
In Amos, justice is restorative: God's righteousness means setting things right for the oppressed. Jesus' ministry carries the same heart, good news to the poor (Luke 4:18), and the Father is known in how we treat "the least of these" (Matt 25:40).

At the Jerusalem council James quotes Amos 9:11–12 to explain the Gentile mission: God has rebuilt David's fallen tent so that "the residue of men might seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles" (Acts 15:16–17). The restored house of David is the risen Christ and his people from every nation.

blocks.subject: entry:book/oba
blocks.body:
Obadiah is a single chapter of 21 verses against Edom, the nation descended from Esau. When Babylon sacked Jerusalem, Edom stood by, looted and handed over fugitives (Obad 1:11–14). Obadiah says that the brother's betrayal will be repaid: "as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee" (Obad 1:15).

The book closes with deliverers on Mount Zion and the line "the kingdom shall be the LORD's" (Obad 1:21).

blocks.subject: entry:book/oba
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Obadiah is about brothers: Jacob and Esau, betrayal instead of family loyalty. The gospel's answer is not endless retaliation but reconciliation. Jesus, the true Israel, makes peace between estranged peoples (Eph 2:14–16). Even Edom (Idumea) appears among the crowds coming to Jesus (Mark 3:8).

"The kingdom shall be the LORD's" (Obad 1:21) is echoed in Rev 11:15: "The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ."

blocks.subject: entry:book/jon
blocks.body:
Jonah is told to preach against Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, and sails the other way. A storm, a great fish and a prayer from its belly bring him back. He preaches, Nineveh repents from king to cattle, and God relents.

Jonah is furious. He explains why he fled: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness" (Jonah 4:2), quoting Exod 34:6 as a complaint. The book ends with God's unanswered question: should I not spare Nineveh, with its 120,000 people "that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand; and also much cattle?" (Jonah 4:11).

blocks.subject: entry:book/jon
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Jonah's problem is that God is too kind, even to enemies. Jesus reveals the same Father who "maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good" and tells us to love our enemies (Matt 5:44–45).

Jesus calls himself the sign of Jonah: "as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matt 12:40). But unlike Jonah, Jesus goes willingly into the deep for the sake of the nations, and rises to send his message of mercy to the whole world.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jon
blocks.title: History or parable?
blocks.body: Many traditional readers take Jonah as history, noting that Jonah is a real prophet (2 Kgs 14:25) and that Jesus mentions Nineveh's repentance alongside the Queen of Sheba (Matt 12:41–42). Many other scholars read it as a didactic story or parable written after the exile to challenge narrow nationalism, pointing to its satire, exaggeration and late Hebrew. Some suggest it combines a historical figure with literary shaping. Its theology of God's mercy stands on either reading.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mic
blocks.body:
Micah, from a village in the Judean lowlands, was a contemporary of Isaiah. He attacks land-grabbing, corrupt judges and prophets for hire. A century later his warning that Zion would be "plowed like a field" (Mic 3:12) was remembered and saved Jeremiah's life (Jer 26:18).

Micah 4 shares with Isaiah the vision of nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD and swords beaten into ploughshares (Mic 4:1–4). Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem as the birthplace of a coming ruler. Micah 6:8 sums up what God asks: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God". The book ends: "Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity... he delighteth in mercy" (Mic 7:18).

blocks.subject: entry:book/mic
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The scribes in Herod's court quote Mic 5:2 to locate the Messiah's birth in Bethlehem (Matt 2:5–6). The ruler "whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting" is the eternal Son, who "shall be great unto the ends of the earth. And this man shall be the peace" (Mic 5:4–5).

Micah's God "delighteth in mercy" (Mic 7:18) and casts sins "into the depths of the sea". This is the Father Jesus reveals. The vision of nations learning peace and swords turned into ploughshares (Mic 4:1–4) describes the kingdom that grows in history as the gospel spreads.

blocks.subject: entry:book/nam
blocks.body:
Nahum (whose name means "comfort") is a poem celebrating the coming fall of Nineveh, which happened in 612 BC to the Babylonians and Medes. Assyria was notorious for cruelty, and Nahum asks: "upon whom hath not thy wickedness passed continually?" (Nah 3:19).

Nahum is a companion to Jonah: Nineveh once repented, but returned to violence. The book holds together God's patience ("slow to anger", Nah 1:3) and his refusal to let oppression win. "The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble" (Nah 1:7).

blocks.subject: entry:book/nam
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Nahum announces "him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace" (Nah 1:15) because the oppressor is broken. Paul uses the parallel line in Isa 52:7 for gospel preaching (Rom 10:15). The good news is that the violent empire does not get the last word.

Through Jesus we see that God's wrath is aimed at what destroys his children: injustice, cruelty, the powers. At the cross Christ defeats the "bloody city" of every age not by out-violencing it but by absorbing its violence and rising.

blocks.subject: entry:book/hab
blocks.body:
Habakkuk complains: why does God tolerate violence in Judah? God answers that he is raising up Babylon. Habakkuk complains again: how can God use a nation worse than Judah? He climbs his watchtower and waits.

God replies: "the just shall live by his faith" (Hab 2:4), and promises that "the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea" (Hab 2:14). The book ends with a psalm: "Although the fig tree shall not blossom... Yet I will rejoice in the LORD" (Hab 3:17–18).

Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a commentary (pesher) on Habakkuk 1–2.

blocks.subject: entry:book/hab
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
"The just shall live by his faith" (Hab 2:4). The Hebrew *emunah* means faithfulness, steady trust. Paul quotes it in Rom 1:17 and Gal 3:11, and Hebrews in Heb 10:38. Many readers see in Paul's use the faithfulness of Christ himself: the faithful Son who trusted the Father through the cross, whose faithfulness we share by union with him.

The promise that the earth will be filled with the knowledge of God's glory "as the waters cover the sea" is the horizon of the gospel age: the kingdom spreading until it covers the earth (compare Isa 11:9).

blocks.subject: entry:book/zep
blocks.body:
Zephaniah, a descendant of King Hezekiah, prophesied under Josiah. His opening is the darkest picture of the day of the LORD in the prophets (Zeph 1:14–18), the basis of the medieval hymn *Dies Irae*. Judgment falls on Judah and the nations.

But the book ends with one of Scripture's most tender pictures: God gathers a humble remnant and "will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing" (Zeph 3:17). God also promises to give the peoples "a pure language" to call on his name (Zeph 3:9).

blocks.subject: entry:book/zep
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The end of Zephaniah is the Father in the parable of the lost son: celebration, music and dancing over a child brought home (Luke 15:25). God's purpose in judgment is to purify and gather, not to destroy.

The "pure language" for the nations (Zeph 3:9) reverses Babel; Pentecost, where every nation hears God's works in its own tongue (Acts 2:6–11), is the beginning of its fulfilment in Christ.

blocks.subject: entry:book/hag
blocks.body: Haggai's four dated messages came in 520 BC. The people had built their own houses but left God's house in ruins (Hag 1:4). They began work within weeks. When the older generation was discouraged by the modest building, Haggai promised: "I am with you" and "The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former... and in this place will I give peace" (Hag 2:4, 9). He ends by calling Zerubbabel, of David's line, God's "signet" (Hag 2:23).

blocks.subject: entry:book/hag
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The rebuilt Second Temple never matched Solomon's in splendour, but the promise came true: Jesus walked in it. The greater glory was the Son in his Father's house (Luke 2:49; John 2:16). God's presence is the point of any temple, and in Jesus that presence is a person. Zerubbabel the signet appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:12–13), and the Son of David is the true seal of the Father's promises.

Hebrews quotes Haggai's shaking of heaven and earth (Hag 2:6; Heb 12:26–28): the old covenant order was being shaken in the first century so that "a kingdom which cannot be moved" might remain.

blocks.subject: entry:book/zec
blocks.body:
Zechariah, Haggai's contemporary, opens with "Turn ye unto me... and I will turn unto you" (Zech 1:3). Eight night visions (Zec 1–6) picture God's protection of Jerusalem, the cleansing of Joshua the high priest (Zec 3) and the Spirit's role: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit" (Zech 4:6).

Chapters 9–14 change style. They announce a king "lowly, and riding upon an ass" (Zech 9:9), a shepherd valued at thirty pieces of silver (Zech 11:12), a pierced one whom the people mourn (Zech 12:10), a fountain for cleansing (Zech 13:1) and the day when "the LORD shall be king over all the earth" (Zech 14:9). The New Testament quotes these chapters heavily in the passion narratives.

blocks.subject: entry:book/zec
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Jesus deliberately enacts Zech 9:9 when he enters Jerusalem on a donkey (Matt 21:4–5): a king of peace who will "speak peace unto the heathen" and rule "from sea even to sea" (Zech 9:10). His kingdom grows without war horses.

The thirty pieces of silver, the struck shepherd and scattered sheep (Zech 13:7; Mark 14:27), and the pierced one (Zech 12:10; John 19:37) are woven into the passion. In Zec 3 the accuser is silenced and the priest's filthy garments are replaced by clean ones: not a courtroom transaction but the LORD rebuking Satan and reclothing his son. Zechariah 14's living waters going out from Jerusalem anticipate the Spirit going out to the nations.

blocks.subject: entry:book/zec
blocks.title: One Zechariah or two?
blocks.body: Chapters 1–8 are dated to 520–518 BC and name Zerubbabel and Joshua. Chapters 9–14 have no dates, a different style and a broader, more apocalyptic outlook; Zech 9:13 mentions Greece. Most scholars therefore treat 9–14 as later oracles attached to Zechariah's book. Conservative scholars argue for unity, noting shared themes (cleansing, Jerusalem's centrality, nations coming to worship) and that Zechariah could have prophesied later in life. Matthew's attribution of Zech 11:12–13 to "Jeremy the prophet" (Matt 27:9), probably because he blends it with Jeremiah's field purchase, is sometimes brought into the discussion.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mal
blocks.body:
Malachi is set out as a series of debates. God speaks, the people object ("Wherein hast thou loved us?"), and God answers. He begins, "I have loved you" (Mal 1:2). He rebukes priests offering blemished sacrifices, men divorcing their wives, and people robbing God in tithes.

God promises to send "my messenger" to prepare the way, followed by "the messenger of the covenant" coming suddenly to his temple (Mal 3:1), and Elijah before "the great and dreadful day of the LORD" (Mal 4:5). In the Christian order of books, Malachi's last words, about turning "the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers" (Mal 4:6), close the Old Testament.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mal
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Malachi begins with love and frames the covenant in family terms: "A son honoureth his father... if then I be a father, where is mine honour?" (Mal 1:6), and "Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?" (Mal 2:10).

Jesus identifies John the Baptist as the promised messenger and Elijah (Matt 11:10–14; Luke 1:17). Jesus is the Lord who comes suddenly to his temple, cleansing it, and the "Sun of righteousness" who rises "with healing in his wings" (Mal 4:2). The last promise of the Old Testament is relational: hearts of fathers and children turned toward each other, the restored family that the Father's Son came to create. The "great and dreadful day" that followed John's ministry is read by partial preterists as AD 70.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mat
blocks.body:
Matthew begins with a genealogy from Abraham through David to Jesus and ends with the risen Jesus sending his disciples to "teach all nations" (Matt 28:19). It is arranged around five large blocks of teaching, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount (Mat 5–7), which many have seen as echoing the five books of Moses.

Matthew quotes the Old Testament more than any other Gospel, often with "that it might be fulfilled". His phrase "kingdom of heaven" is a reverent Jewish way of saying "kingdom of God". The Olivet Discourse (Mat 24–25) answers the disciples' question about the temple's destruction.

The Gospel was the most used Gospel in the early church and stood first in nearly every early list.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mat
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Matthew's Jesus is "Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us" (Matt 1:23), and the Gospel ends with "lo, I am with you alway" (Matt 28:20). Presence frames everything.

Jesus teaches his disciples to pray "Our Father" and to be "perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect" (Matt 5:48), a perfection defined by the Father's kindness to the unthankful (Matt 5:45). He relives Israel's story: out of Egypt, through the waters, tested in the wilderness, faithful where Israel faltered.

The Olivet Discourse answers the disciples' question about the temple (Matt 24:1–3) and insists "This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled" (Matt 24:34). A partial-preterist reading takes this at face value: the "coming" of the Son of Man in judgment was fulfilled in AD 70, when the old covenant order ended. The Great Commission then rests on a present reality: "All power is given unto me in heaven and in earth" (Matt 28:18). The nations are to be discipled because Christ already reigns.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mat
blocks.title: Who wrote Matthew, and when?
blocks.body:
**The Synoptic problem.** Matthew, Mark and Luke share much material, often word for word. Most scholars hold that Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke each used Mark plus a sayings source called "Q" (the Two-Source hypothesis). Others argue Luke used Matthew as well as Mark (the Farrer hypothesis), or that Matthew came first (the Griesbach or Two-Gospel hypothesis, closer to the early church's order). Dating each Gospel depends partly on which order is accepted.

**Authorship.** Early church writers unanimously name the apostle Matthew. Supporters note that only this Gospel calls the converted tax collector "Matthew" (Matt 9:9; compare Mark 2:14) and has a special interest in money and taxes. Most critical scholars think an apostle would not have relied so heavily on Mark and see the author as a learned Jewish-Christian teacher (compare Matt 13:52).

**Date.** If Matthew used Mark, most place it c. 80–90, some reading Matt 22:7 ("burned up their city") as written after AD 70. Others reply that burning a rebel city was a stock image and that Matthew's instructions about temple offerings and the temple tax assume it still stands, favouring a date before 70. The early date is a minority view.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mat
blocks.title: Irenaeus on the four Gospels
blocks.body: Writing around AD 180, Irenaeus said that Matthew issued a Gospel among the Hebrews in their own dialect while Peter and Paul were preaching in Rome; that after their departure Mark, Peter's disciple and interpreter, handed down Peter's preaching in writing; that Luke, Paul's companion, recorded the gospel Paul preached; and that John, the disciple who leaned on the Lord's breast, published his Gospel while living at Ephesus. This is the earliest surviving explicit statement of all four authors.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mat
blocks.title: Papias on Matthew
blocks.body: Papias also said that Matthew put together "the oracles" (*logia*) in the Hebrew (or Aramaic) language, and each person interpreted them as best he could. Scholars disagree about whether he meant our Greek Matthew, an earlier Semitic collection of sayings, or a Gospel written in a Jewish style.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mrk
blocks.body:
Mark is fast-paced; the word "straightway" (immediately) appears dozens of times. It opens, "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" (Mark 1:1), and at the cross a Roman centurion confesses, "Truly this man was the Son of God" (Mark 15:39). The disciples rarely understand, and Jesus often tells people not to spread news of him (the "messianic secret").

The turning point is Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:29), after which Jesus three times predicts his death. Mark explains Jewish customs for non-Jewish readers (Mark 7:3–4) and uses Latin loanwords, fitting a Roman setting.

The oldest complete manuscripts end at Mark 16:8, with the women fleeing the tomb in fear; the longer ending (Mark 16:9–20) is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mrk
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Mark's key verse is Mark 10:45: "the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many." In Mark's world a ransom is the price of freeing captives. Jesus binds "the strong man" and plunders his house (Mark 3:27): his death is the rescue of hostages from the powers, the Christus Victor heart of the gospel, not a payment to the Father.

At Jesus' baptism the heavens are torn open and the Father speaks, "Thou art my beloved Son" (Mark 1:11). At his death the temple veil is torn (Mark 15:38), the same verb: God's presence breaks out to everyone. In Gethsemane Jesus prays "Abba, Father" (Mark 14:36), the intimate prayer he shares with his followers by the Spirit (Rom 8:15). Mrk 13 prepares disciples for Jerusalem's fall within "this generation" (Mark 13:30).

blocks.subject: entry:book/mrk
blocks.title: When was Mark written?
blocks.body:
Most scholars date Mark to c. 65–73. They connect its stress on suffering to Nero's persecution in Rome (64) and read Mrk 13 as written during the Jewish War (66–70), either just before or just after the temple fell. Early tradition differs on whether Mark wrote while Peter was alive (Clement of Alexandria, via Eusebius) or after Peter and Paul's "departure" (Irenaeus).

A minority date Mark in the 40s or 50s, arguing that Luke–Acts was written by c. 62 and used Mark. Some also note that Mrk 13 lacks the details of the siege one might expect after the event.

blocks.subject: entry:book/mrk
blocks.title: Papias on Mark
blocks.body: Papias, bishop of Hierapolis in the early 2nd century, passed on what "the elder" told him: Mark had been Peter's interpreter and wrote down accurately, though not in order, what he remembered of the Lord's words and deeds as Peter taught them. Papias' own books are lost; Eusebius preserves this passage.

blocks.subject: entry:book/luk
blocks.body:
Luke opens like a Greek historian: he has investigated "all things from the very first" and writes "in order" so that Theophilus may know the certainty of what he was taught (Luke 1:1–4). He dates events by Roman rulers (Luke 2:1; 3:1).

About half of Luke is unique to it, including the shepherds, the Magnificat, the Good Samaritan, the lost sheep, coin and son (Luk 15), Zacchaeus and the road to Emmaus. Women, the poor, Samaritans and sinners are prominent. The long journey to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51–19:27) holds much of Jesus' teaching. Luke is the first of two volumes; Acts continues the story.

blocks.subject: entry:book/luk
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Luke 15 is the Bible's clearest picture of the Father. The father runs to the returning son, embraces him before he finishes his confession and restores him as a son (Luke 15:20–24), and then goes out to plead with the angry elder brother. Salvation here is a homecoming, not a transaction.

Jesus' first sermon announces release for captives and "the acceptable year of the Lord" (Luke 4:18–19), the Jubilee. On the cross he forgives his executioners (Luke 23:34) and welcomes a thief (Luke 23:43), and dies saying "Father, into thy hands" (Luke 23:46). Luke's genealogy ends "which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God" (Luke 3:38): Jesus restores humanity's sonship.

Luke's version of the Olivet Discourse is explicit that "Jerusalem compassed with armies" is the sign of "the desolation thereof" (Luke 21:20), anchoring the discourse in the events of AD 70.

blocks.subject: entry:book/luk
blocks.title: When was Luke written?
blocks.body: Luke–Acts is a two-volume work, so its date depends on Acts. Most scholars place Luke c. 80–90: it seems to use Mark, and Luke 21:20–24 describes Jerusalem surrounded by armies more specifically than Mark does. A minority argue that Acts ends abruptly with Paul alive in Rome (c. 62), so Luke must be earlier. A further minority date Luke–Acts into the early 2nd century. See the essay "Dating the New Testament".

blocks.subject: entry:book/luk
blocks.title: Irenaeus on the four Gospels
blocks.body: Writing around AD 180, Irenaeus said that Matthew issued a Gospel among the Hebrews in their own dialect while Peter and Paul were preaching in Rome; that after their departure Mark, Peter's disciple and interpreter, handed down Peter's preaching in writing; that Luke, Paul's companion, recorded the gospel Paul preached; and that John, the disciple who leaned on the Lord's breast, published his Gospel while living at Ephesus. Irenaeus also used Acts' 'we' passages to show Luke was Paul's companion.

blocks.subject: entry:book/luk
blocks.title: The Muratorian fragment on Luke
blocks.body: The Muratorian fragment, an early list of New Testament books, names Luke the physician, Paul's companion, as the author of the third Gospel and of the Acts of all the apostles. The fragment's own date is debated (see the essay "How the canon formed").

citations.ref: Muratorian fragment, on Luke and Acts

blocks.subject: entry:book/jhn
blocks.body:
John differs from the other Gospels. It records seven signs (miracles) and long discourses, includes several trips to Jerusalem over at least three Passovers, and contains the "I am" sayings: bread of life, light of the world, good shepherd, resurrection and life, way, truth and life, true vine.

Its prologue (John 1:1–18) identifies Jesus as the eternal Word who "was made flesh, and dwelt among us". Chapters 13–17, the Upper Room discourse, are Jesus' longest teaching to his disciples, ending with his prayer to the Father. The Gospel states its purpose plainly: "that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name" (John 20:31).

The earliest New Testament fragment, P52, comes from John 18.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jhn
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
John is the source of "Jesus is perfect theology". "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him" (John 1:18). "He that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (John 14:9). Whatever we think God is like, we test it against Jesus.

Eternal life is relational: "this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ" (John 17:3). Jesus prays that his disciples will be one "as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us" (John 17:21): salvation is being drawn into the life the Father and Son share in the Spirit. He calls his disciples friends (John 15:15) and after the resurrection says, "I ascend unto my Father, and your Father" (John 20:17): his Father is now theirs.

The cross is the hour when "the prince of this world" is cast out and Jesus draws all to himself (John 12:31–32).

blocks.subject: entry:book/jhn
blocks.title: Who was the beloved disciple?
blocks.body:
The Gospel claims to rest on the testimony of "the disciple whom Jesus loved" (John 21:20–24), and the closing "we know that his testimony is true" suggests others helped publish it.

- **John son of Zebedee:** the traditional view, from Irenaeus onward. Zebedee's sons are never named in John, which fits an author keeping himself in the background.
- **Another disciple:** some argue the beloved disciple was a Jerusalem follower, not one of the Twelve, possibly the "elder John" mentioned by Papias, or Lazarus ("he whom thou lovest", John 11:3).
- **Community authorship:** many critical scholars see the Gospel as shaped over time by a community gathered around the beloved disciple's witness.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jhn
blocks.title: Irenaeus on the four Gospels
blocks.body: Writing around AD 180, Irenaeus said that Matthew issued a Gospel among the Hebrews in their own dialect while Peter and Paul were preaching in Rome; that after their departure Mark, Peter's disciple and interpreter, handed down Peter's preaching in writing; that Luke, Paul's companion, recorded the gospel Paul preached; and that John, the disciple who leaned on the Lord's breast, published his Gospel while living at Ephesus. Irenaeus had known Polycarp, who he said had known John.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jhn
blocks.title: Clement of Alexandria: the 'spiritual Gospel'
blocks.body: Clement of Alexandria, as quoted by Eusebius, said that John, last of all, seeing that the bodily facts had been set out in the other Gospels, was urged by his friends and inspired by the Spirit to compose a "spiritual Gospel".

blocks.subject: entry:book/act
blocks.body:
Acts continues Luke's Gospel. Jesus tells his disciples, "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth" (Acts 1:8), and the book follows that map. The Spirit comes at Pentecost (Act 2), the church grows in Jerusalem, Stephen is killed, Philip goes to Samaria and Saul the persecutor meets the risen Jesus.

Peter's vision and the Spirit falling on Cornelius' household (Act 10) open the door to Gentiles, and the Jerusalem council confirms that Gentiles need not be circumcised (Act 15). The second half follows Paul's missionary journeys, arrest and voyage to Rome. The book ends with Paul in Rome "preaching the kingdom of God... with all confidence, no man forbidding him" (Acts 28:31).

blocks.subject: entry:book/act
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Acts is really "the acts of the risen Jesus by his Spirit". Luke says his first book was about "all that Jesus began both to do and teach" (Acts 1:1); Acts is what he continues to do. The ascension is an enthronement: Peter declares Jesus has been made "both Lord and Christ" and sits at God's right hand until his enemies are made his footstool (Acts 2:33–36). The kingdom has begun, and it spreads not by force but by witness, suffering and the Spirit.

The family of God widens: Ethiopians, Samaritans, Romans and Greeks are brought in. Paul tells the Athenians that we are all God's "offspring" (Acts 17:28–29) and calls them to know the Father whom they have been seeking. Postmillennial readers see Acts as the first chapter of a story in which the mustard seed becomes a tree.

blocks.subject: entry:book/act
blocks.title: Why does Acts end where it does?
blocks.body:
Acts ends with Paul alive under house arrest in Rome for "two whole years" (Acts 28:30), around AD 62. It does not mention Nero's persecution (64), the deaths of James (62), Peter or Paul (mid-60s), or the destruction of Jerusalem (70).

**Early-date argument (minority):** the simplest explanation is that Luke wrote at that point, around 62–64. This would place Luke's Gospel, and probably Mark, earlier still.

**Majority response:** Acts ends where its story is complete: the gospel has reached Rome "unhindered". Luke may have avoided Paul's death for literary or apologetic reasons, and Paul's farewell speech already hints at it (Acts 20:25, 38). Most date Acts c. 80–90; a minority argue for the early 2nd century.

See the essay "Dating the New Testament".

blocks.subject: entry:book/rom
blocks.body:
Paul wrote Romans from Corinth around AD 56–57 to churches he had not founded. Emperor Claudius had expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49 (compare Acts 18:2), and when they returned, Jewish and Gentile believers had to learn to live together. Paul hoped Rome would support his mission to Spain (Rom 15:24).

The letter announces the gospel as "the power of God unto salvation... to the Jew first, and also to the Greek" (Rom 1:16). It describes humanity's slide into idolatry and death, God's righteousness revealed through Jesus' faithfulness, the contrast between Adam and Christ, life in the Spirit, God's faithfulness to Israel (Rom 9–11) and practical love among believers (Rom 12–15). Chapter 16 names many co-workers, including women such as Phoebe, Prisca and Junia.

blocks.subject: entry:book/rom
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Romans 8 is the summit: "ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God" (Rom 8:15–16). The goal of the gospel is sonship: to be "conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren" (Rom 8:29).

Paul's frame is union. We are baptised into Christ's death and raised in his life (Rom 6:3–5). Christ is the new Adam who undoes Adam's ruin (Rom 5:12–21). "Sin" and "Death" are tyrants from which we are set free, and creation itself waits for "the glorious liberty of the children of God" (Rom 8:21). Nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ (Rom 8:38–39). Even Israel's stumbling serves the Father's plan to "have mercy upon all" (Rom 11:32).

blocks.subject: entry:book/rom
blocks.title: How the legal reading of Romans arose
blocks.body:
Western Christianity came to read Romans mainly as a courtroom drama: humans are guilty, God the judge must punish, Christ bears the penalty, and believers are declared righteous by imputation.

- **Latin vocabulary.** Translating *dikaiosynē* and *dikaioō* as *iustitia* and *iustificare* tied Paul's words to Roman legal categories.
- **Augustine** read Romans through grace and original sin, shaping the Western framework.
- **Anselm** described sin as failing to give God the honour due to him, requiring satisfaction, a framework rooted in feudal honour.
- **The Reformation.** Luther found peace in justification by faith alone. **Calvin** defined justification as God's acceptance of us as righteous through the forgiveness of sins and the imputation of Christ's righteousness.
- **Charles Hodge** and later Reformed theology systematised a forensic, penal view.

**How the relational authors read it:** "the righteousness of God" (Rom 1:17; 3:21) is God's own faithfulness to his covenant and his saving action to set the world right. Justification is God welcoming people into his family, the one people promised to Abraham, on the basis of Christ's faithfulness; Rom 5–8 moves from peace with God to adoption, union with Christ and the Spirit crying "Abba". This app reads Romans that way.

blocks.subject: entry:book/rom
blocks.title: N. T. Wright on justification
blocks.body: N. T. Wright argues that in Paul "the righteousness of God" means God's own faithfulness to his covenant promises to Abraham, through which he will put the world right. Justification is God's declaration about who belongs to his one covenant family, Jew and Gentile together, marked by faith in Jesus. He sees this as rooted in God's plan rather than as a primarily individual courtroom transaction. He develops this especially from Romans 3–4.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1co
blocks.body:
Corinth was a Roman colony refounded in 44 BC, a busy port city proud of status and rhetoric. Paul founded the church around AD 50–52. The Gallio inscription at Delphi helps date his stay (Acts 18:12).

1 Corinthians responds to reports and a letter from the church (1 Cor 7:1). Factions have formed around leaders; the rich humiliate the poor at the Lord's Supper (1 Cor 11:21–22); members sue each other; questions arise about sex, marriage, idol food, worship and spiritual gifts. Paul answers with the cross, which turns worldly status upside down (1 Cor 1:18–31), the image of the church as Christ's body (1Co 12), the hymn to love (1Co 13) and the earliest written account of the resurrection appearances (1 Cor 15:3–8).

blocks.subject: entry:book/1co
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Paul determined to know nothing "save Jesus Christ, and him crucified" (1 Cor 2:2), because the cross reveals what God is like: power made known in weakness, wisdom in what looks like folly.

1 Corinthians 15 is a Christus Victor chapter. Christ is the firstfruits of the resurrection and the second Adam (1 Cor 15:22, 45). "He must reign, till he hath put all enemies under his feet. The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death" (1 Cor 15:25–26): Christ reigns now, and his reign progresses through history until death itself is undone. The goal is "that God may be all in all" (1 Cor 15:28). Love, which "never faileth" (1 Cor 13:8), is the life of the Trinity shared with us.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2co
blocks.body:
After writing 1 Corinthians, Paul made a "painful" visit and wrote a severe letter (2 Cor 2:1–4). Titus brought news that many had responded, but rival teachers ("super-apostles") were undermining Paul. 2 Corinthians mixes relief, defence, appeal and irony.

Many scholars think it combines several letters, since chapters 10–13 are so much sharper than 1–9. Paul speaks of the treasure of the gospel "in earthen vessels" (2 Cor 4:7), urges generosity for Jerusalem's poor (2Co 8–9) and boasts of his weaknesses, including a "thorn in the flesh" (2 Cor 12:7–10).

blocks.subject: entry:book/2co
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
"God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them" (2 Cor 5:19). The Father is not the one who needs reconciling; he is the reconciler, present in Christ, healing the estrangement from his side.

We behold "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor 4:6): Jesus is perfect theology. Being in him is new creation (2 Cor 5:17), and beholding his glory we are "changed into the same image" from glory to glory (2 Cor 3:18). Christ "became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich" (2 Cor 8:9), the self-giving of the Trinity turned outward. And God says "I will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters" (2 Cor 6:18).

blocks.subject: entry:book/gal
blocks.body:
Galatians is Paul's most heated letter. After he planted churches in Galatia, other teachers insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to belong to God's people. Paul skips his usual thanksgiving and goes straight to defending his gospel and his calling (Gal 1:6–2:10).

He recounts confronting Peter at Antioch for withdrawing from table fellowship with Gentiles (Gal 2:11–14), argues from Abraham that the promise came by faith (Gal 3), and declares: "There is neither Jew nor Greek... bond nor free... male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28). The letter ends with the fruit of the Spirit (Gal 5:22–23) and "a new creature" (Gal 6:15).

blocks.subject: entry:book/gal
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Galatians is a letter about adoption. "When the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son... to redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons. And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father" (Gal 4:4–6). Redemption here is release from slavery into sonship (*huiothesia*): the slave becomes an heir (Gal 4:7).

The question at Antioch was who may eat at the family table. Paul's answer is union: "I am crucified with Christ... Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20). Life comes "by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me". The Christ who "delivers us from this present evil age" (Gal 1:4) is the victor over the powers that once enslaved us (Gal 4:3, 9).

blocks.subject: entry:book/gal
blocks.title: Which Galatians, and when?
blocks.body:
"Galatia" could mean the ethnic region of the Celtic Galatians in north-central Anatolia, or the larger Roman province, which included Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, cities Paul visited on his first journey (Act 13–14).

- **South Galatian, early (c. 48–49):** written before the Jerusalem council of Act 15; this would make Galatians Paul's earliest letter and explains why he never cites the council's decision.
- **South Galatian, after the council (c. 50–55).**
- **North Galatian (c. 53–57):** the traditional view in older commentaries, linking Galatians closely in time to Romans.

Scholars are divided; the South Galatian view is widely held among those who give weight to Acts.

blocks.subject: entry:book/gal
blocks.title: N. T. Wright on justification
blocks.body: N. T. Wright argues that in Paul "the righteousness of God" means God's own faithfulness to his covenant promises to Abraham, through which he will put the world right. Justification is God's declaration about who belongs to his one covenant family, Jew and Gentile together, marked by faith in Jesus. He sees this as rooted in God's plan rather than as a primarily individual courtroom transaction. In Galatians he stresses the question of table fellowship at Antioch.
