blocks.subject: entry:book/gal
blocks.title: How the legal reading of Galatians arose
blocks.body:
Galatians became, with Romans, the charter of the Reformation. Read through Latin *iustificatio*, "justified by faith" (Gal 2:16) was heard as a courtroom verdict on an individual conscience burdened by guilt, with "works of the law" understood as human efforts to earn God's favour.

Read in its own setting, Galatians is about table fellowship and family membership: whether Gentiles must become Jews to belong to Abraham's family. "Works of the law" refers especially to markers like circumcision, food laws and calendar. Paul's answer is adoption by the Spirit and union with the crucified and risen Son. The legal reading captures that grace is a gift, but it misses that the gift is a family.

blocks.subject: entry:book/eph
blocks.body:
Ephesians reads more like a sermon or prayer than a reply to a crisis. Some early manuscripts (including P46, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) lack "at Ephesus" in Eph 1:1, so many think it was a circular letter for several churches.

The first half praises God for blessings "in Christ" (a phrase repeated throughout), then explains how Gentiles once "far off" have been brought near and Jew and Gentile made "one new man" (Eph 2:15). The second half calls the church to walk worthy of that calling: unity, gifts, truthful speech, a Spirit-filled household and spiritual armour against "principalities" and "powers" (Eph 6:12).

blocks.subject: entry:book/eph
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Ephesians opens with the Father's purpose before creation: "having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will" (Eph 1:5). Election is adoption; God's plan is a family. His aim is "to gather together in one all things in Christ" (Eph 1:10).

The risen Christ is seated "far above all principality, and power" with all things under his feet (Eph 1:20–22), and we are seated with him (Eph 2:6). The cross "abolished the enmity" between peoples and made peace (Eph 2:14–16). Paul prays that we may know "the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge" and be filled "with all the fulness of God" (Eph 3:19), and bows "unto the Father... of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named" (Eph 3:14–15).

blocks.subject: entry:book/eph
blocks.title: Did Paul write Ephesians?
blocks.body:
**For Paul's authorship:** The letter claims Paul as author and was accepted from the earliest period. Differences in style can be explained by its liturgical, prayer-like character, by a secretary, or by Paul writing a general letter rather than answering a problem.

**Against (pseudonymous, written by a follower in Paul's name):** Very long sentences (Eph 1:3–14 is one sentence in Greek), distinctive vocabulary, close dependence on Colossians, and a church-wide (universal) view of the church differ from the undisputed letters.

Most critical scholars regard Ephesians as post-Pauline; many conservative scholars defend Paul's authorship. Pseudonymous writing in a teacher's name was known in the ancient world, but whether the early church would have accepted it knowingly is itself debated.

blocks.subject: entry:book/php
blocks.body:
Philippi was a Roman colony in Macedonia, settled by veterans and proud of its Roman status. Paul founded the church on his second journey (Act 16): Lydia the merchant, a slave girl and a jailer were among the first converts.

Writing from prison, Paul thanks the church for its gift and its long partnership. Joy is the keynote despite chains. At the centre is the Christ hymn (Phil 2:5–11): Christ did not grasp equality with God but emptied himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death on a cross, and God exalted him. Paul tells the colony-dwellers that "our conversation [citizenship] is in heaven" (Phil 3:20).

blocks.subject: entry:book/php
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The Christ hymn is perfect theology in a few lines: being "in the form of God" looks like self-giving. Jesus does not empty himself in spite of being God but precisely as the revelation of God. The Father's glory is the glory of humble, serving love, and "every knee should bow" before that kind of Lord (Phil 2:10–11).

Paul's goal is relational: "That I may know him, and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings" (Phil 3:10). He longs to be "found in him" (Phil 3:9). In a Roman colony that honoured Caesar as lord and saviour, Paul names Jesus as the true Saviour whose kingdom will transform all things (Phil 3:20–21).

blocks.subject: entry:book/php
blocks.title: Where was Paul imprisoned?
blocks.body: Paul writes from prison but does not say where. The **Roman** imprisonment (c. 60–62) is the traditional and majority view, supported by references to the "palace" (praetorium) and "Caesar's household". An **Ephesian** imprisonment (c. 54–55) is suggested because several journeys between Paul and Philippi seem to happen during his confinement, which is easier from nearby Ephesus. A **Caesarean** setting (c. 57–59) is a third option. The choice affects the date by up to seven years but not the letter's meaning.

blocks.subject: entry:book/col
blocks.body:
Colossae was a minor town in the Lycus valley near Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul had not visited; Epaphras founded the church (Col 1:7). A "philosophy" was urging believers toward visions, angel worship, food rules and special days (Col 2:8, 16–18).

Paul responds with one of the New Testament's highest statements about Christ (Col 1:15–20): the image of the invisible God, firstborn over creation, the one in whom all things hold together. Because believers are complete in him, they need no extra spiritual ladder. The letter shares many co-workers and the slave Onesimus with Philemon (Col 4:9).

blocks.subject: entry:book/col
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
"He is the image of the invisible God" (Col 1:15). The God no one has seen is shown in Jesus; "in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (Col 2:9). This is the foundation for reading all Scripture through Jesus.

Colossians gives the clearest Christus Victor statement in Paul: God "blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us... nailing it to his cross; and having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it" (Col 2:14–15). The cross is a victory parade over the powers. Through Christ God reconciles "all things unto himself... having made peace through the blood of his cross" (Col 1:20). Our life is "hid with Christ in God" (Col 3:3): union, not merely pardon.

blocks.subject: entry:book/col
blocks.title: Did Paul write Colossians?
blocks.body:
**For Paul's authorship:** Its personal greetings and co-workers match Philemon closely, and its theology grows naturally from Paul's in the undisputed letters.

**Against (pseudonymous, written by a follower in Paul's name):** Its style is different (long chains of genitives and clauses), its picture of Christ as head of a cosmic body is more developed, and it speaks of believers already raised with Christ (Col 3:1).

Scholarship is roughly divided; a sizeable group of critical scholars accept it as Paul's or written by a co-worker such as Timothy during his lifetime. Pseudonymous writing in a teacher's name was known in the ancient world, but whether the early church would have accepted it knowingly is itself debated.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1th
blocks.body:
1 Thessalonians is probably the earliest Christian writing we have (unless Galatians is earlier). Paul had to leave Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia, after a few weeks because of opposition (Act 17). Worried, he sent Timothy, who returned with good news. Paul writes with relief and affection, "as a nurse cherisheth her children" (1 Thess 2:7) and as "a father doth his children" (1 Thess 2:11).

Believers had "turned to God from idols" (1 Thess 1:9), but some had died, and the others were unsure what this meant. Paul answers that "the dead in Christ shall rise first" when the Lord comes (1 Thess 4:13–18).

blocks.subject: entry:book/1th
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Paul's comfort to the grieving is relational: "so shall we ever be with the Lord" (1 Thess 4:17). The goal of the Lord's coming is unbroken presence.

The word "coming" (*parousia*) was used for the arrival of a king or emperor to a city, when citizens went out to "meet" him and escort him back in (the same word, *apantēsis*, in 1 Thess 4:17). The picture is not escape from the earth but welcoming the King who comes to reign. Paul calls the church to live now as children of light (1 Thess 5:5), and the "wrath to come" from which Jesus delivers us (1 Thess 1:10) is the destructive end of a world in rebellion, not the Father's hostility toward his children.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2th
blocks.body:
2 Thessalonians addresses confusion caused by a report, perhaps a forged letter (2 Thess 2:2), that the day of the Lord had already arrived. Paul says a falling away and the revelation of "that man of sin" who sits "in the temple of God" must come first, and that something or someone is currently restraining him (2 Thess 2:3–7).

He also rebukes members who had stopped working and were living off others: "if any would not work, neither should he eat" (2 Thess 3:10).

blocks.subject: entry:book/2th
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Paul assures persecuted believers that God sees their suffering and will set things right (2 Thess 1:5–7). Justice here protects God's children.

Partial-preterist interpreters read the "man of sin" sitting in the temple of God (2 Thess 2:4) as a first-century figure connected with the Jewish War and the temple still standing when Paul wrote, with the events of AD 66–70 as the context. Others see a future figure. Either way, the "Lord shall consume [him] with the spirit of his mouth" (2 Thess 2:8): Christ conquers with his word, and the church is to stand firm, keep working and not be shaken.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2th
blocks.title: Did Paul write 2 Thessalonians?
blocks.body:
**For Paul's authorship:** The letter claims Paul's signature (2 Thess 3:17), was accepted early, and its similarity to 1 Thessalonians fits a follow-up written weeks later to the same church.

**Against (pseudonymous, written by a follower in Paul's name):** It copies the structure and wording of 1 Thessalonians closely, yet seems to teach that signs must precede the Lord's coming where 1 Thessalonians stresses suddenness; its tone is cooler.

Scholarship is divided; many scholars still accept Paul's authorship. Pseudonymous writing in a teacher's name was known in the ancient world, but whether the early church would have accepted it knowingly is itself debated.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1ti
blocks.body:
Paul has left Timothy in Ephesus to stop certain people teaching "fables and endless genealogies" (1 Tim 1:3–4). The letter gives instructions on prayer, conduct in worship, qualifications for overseers and deacons (character more than skills), care for widows and the dangers of the love of money (1 Tim 6:10).

The letter contains several short creedal sayings marked "This is a faithful saying" and a hymn: "God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit... received up into glory" (1 Tim 3:16).

blocks.subject: entry:book/1ti
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
1 Timothy is clear about the Father's heart: "God our Saviour; who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth" (1 Tim 2:3–4). There is "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; who gave himself a ransom for all" (1 Tim 2:5–6). He mediates as one of us, a man, joining humanity and God in his own person.

Paul calls himself the chief of sinners who received mercy so that Christ could show "all longsuffering" (1 Tim 1:15–16). The living God "is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe" (1 Tim 4:10).

blocks.subject: entry:book/1ti
blocks.title: Did Paul write the Pastoral Letters?
blocks.body:
**For Paul's authorship:** The letters claim Paul as author and contain detailed personal notes (cloak, books and parchments, named co-workers) that seem odd for a forger. Differences in style may come from a secretary, a different subject (church order) and Paul's age. Paul's travels in them fit a release after Act 28 and a second imprisonment.

**Against (pseudonymous, written by a follower in Paul's name):** About a third of the vocabulary is absent from the other Pauline letters; church offices look more structured; 'faith' often means the body of teaching; they are missing from P46, the earliest collection of Paul's letters (though the manuscript is incomplete), and Marcion did not include them.

Most critical scholars treat 1–2 Timothy and Titus as pseudonymous; some see 2 Timothy as more likely authentic than the other two; many conservative scholars defend Paul's authorship of all three. Pseudonymous writing in a teacher's name was known in the ancient world, but whether the early church would have accepted it knowingly is itself debated.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2ti
blocks.body:
2 Timothy reads as Paul's last testament. He is in prison, most of his companions have left, and he expects execution: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith" (2 Tim 4:7). He asks Timothy to come before winter and bring his cloak, books and parchments (2 Tim 4:13, 21).

He urges Timothy to stir up God's gift, entrust the teaching to faithful people (2 Tim 2:2), and hold to Scripture, which is "given by inspiration of God" (literally God-breathed) and makes one "wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus" (2 Tim 3:15–16).

blocks.subject: entry:book/2ti
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Grace was "given us in Christ Jesus before the world began", and Christ "hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" (2 Tim 1:9–10). Death is not satisfied but abolished: Christus Victor.

Union holds even in failure: "If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself" (2 Tim 2:13). The Scriptures are given to make us wise "through faith which is in Christ Jesus" (2 Tim 3:15): they lead to him.

blocks.title: Did Paul write the Pastoral Letters?
blocks.body:

Differences in style may come from a secretary, a different subject (church order) and Paul's age. Paul's travels in them fit a release after Act 28 and a second imprisonment.

blocks.subject: entry:book/tit
blocks.body:
Titus was left in Crete to "set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city" (Titus 1:5). Paul quotes a Cretan poet on Cretans' reputation (Titus 1:12) and urges sound teaching and good works in every household role.

Two compact summaries of the gospel stand out: "the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, teaching us..." (Titus 2:11–14) and "after that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared" (Titus 3:4–7).

blocks.subject: entry:book/tit
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
"The kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man [*philanthrōpia*] appeared": Jesus is the appearing of God's kindness (Titus 3:4). Salvation is "by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost; which he shed on us abundantly" so that we might be "heirs" (Titus 3:5–7): new birth into a family inheritance.

Grace is not only pardon but a teacher, training us to live (Titus 2:11–12). Christ "gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people" (Titus 2:14): rescue from bondage into belonging.

blocks.title: Did Paul write the Pastoral Letters?
blocks.body:
**For Paul's authorship:** The letters claim Paul as author and contain detailed personal notes (cloak, books and parchments, named co-workers) that seem odd for a forger. blocks.subject: entry:book/phm
blocks.body:
Onesimus, a slave of Philemon in Colossae, had come to Paul, perhaps as a runaway or seeking Paul's help as a mediator in a household dispute. He became a believer, and Paul sends him back with this letter. Paul could command, but appeals "for love's sake" (Phlm 1:9), offers to pay any debt himself (Phlm 1:18–19) and hints Philemon will do "more than I say" (Phlm 1:21).

The letter's name-play is gentle: Onesimus means "useful", once "unprofitable" but now "profitable" (Phlm 1:11).

blocks.subject: entry:book/phm
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Philemon is reconciliation in miniature. Paul stands between the wronged and the wrongdoer and says, "If he hath wronged thee... put that on mine account" (Phlm 1:18), and "receive him as myself" (Phlm 1:17). That is restorative justice: the goal is not punishment but a restored relationship, with the mediator absorbing the cost.

In Christ a slave becomes "a brother beloved" (Phlm 1:16). The gospel creates a family that reorders even the deepest social divisions, and over time this logic undermined slavery itself.

blocks.subject: entry:book/heb
blocks.body:
Hebrews calls itself "the word of exhortation" (Heb 13:22): a sermon with a letter ending. It does not name its author. It compares Jesus with angels, Moses, Joshua, the Levitical priests and the old covenant sacrifices, and each time says Jesus is "better". The aim is pastoral: do not drift away (Heb 2:1), draw near with confidence (Heb 4:16; 10:22).

Its argument relies heavily on the Psalms (especially Psa 110) and Jer 31. Hebrews 11 lists heroes of faith from Abel to the prophets. Hebrews 12 calls readers to run the race "looking unto Jesus", and declares that "we receiving a kingdom which cannot be moved" (Heb 12:28) while the old order is shaken.

blocks.subject: entry:book/heb
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Hebrews opens with Jesus as perfect theology: God, who spoke in fragments through the prophets, "hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son... the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person" (Heb 1:1–3). The Son is the exact imprint of the Father.

The Son shares our flesh "that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil; and deliver them" (Heb 2:14–15): Christus Victor and solidarity together. He is "not ashamed to call them brethren" (Heb 2:11) and brings "many sons unto glory" (Heb 2:10). His priesthood is about access: the veil is opened and we may draw near (Heb 10:19–22).

Hebrews speaks of the old covenant as "ready to vanish away" (Heb 8:13). A partial-preterist reading sees that fulfilled in AD 70, after which the kingdom "which cannot be moved" remains.

blocks.subject: entry:book/heb
blocks.title: Who wrote Hebrews?
blocks.body:
The early church disagreed. The Eastern church (Alexandria) generally counted Hebrews as Paul's, while acknowledging its different style. The Western church was slower to accept it, partly because its authorship was uncertain; it was widely accepted as Paul's in the West by the late 4th century.

Today almost all scholars agree Paul did not write it: its Greek is the most polished in the New Testament, its method of argument differs, and its author says the message "was confirmed unto us by them that heard him" (Heb 2:3), something Paul insisted he did not depend on (Gal 1:12). Suggestions include Barnabas, Apollos (eloquent and from Alexandria, Acts 18:24), Luke, Silas and Priscilla. None can be proved.

blocks.subject: entry:book/heb
blocks.title: Before or after AD 70?
blocks.body:
Hebrews speaks of priests who "offer gifts according to the law" (Heb 8:4) and sacrifices "offered year by year" (Heb 10:1–2) in the present tense, and of the old covenant "ready to vanish away" (Heb 8:13). Many scholars think it was written before AD 70: a writer arguing that the old sacrifices were obsolete would surely have mentioned the temple's destruction.

Others note that Hebrews always discusses the wilderness tabernacle, not the Herodian temple, so its present tenses may be literary, and Josephus also describes the temple cult in the present tense after 70. 1 Clement (c. AD 96) appears to use Hebrews, setting a latest date. Scholars are divided, with a pre-70 date widely held.

blocks.subject: entry:book/heb
blocks.title: Origen: 'God knows'
blocks.body: Origen judged that the thoughts of Hebrews are Paul's but the style and composition belong to someone who recalled the apostle's teaching. He reported traditions naming Clement of Rome or Luke, and concluded that who actually wrote the letter, God knows.

blocks.subject: entry:book/heb
blocks.title: Tertullian: Barnabas
blocks.body: Tertullian cited a passage of Hebrews (Heb 6:4–8) as the work of Barnabas, Paul's companion and a Levite (Acts 4:36), in his argument about repentance.

blocks.subject: entry:book/heb
blocks.title: Clement of Alexandria: Paul, translated by Luke
blocks.body: Clement of Alexandria, as reported by Eusebius, held that Paul wrote Hebrews in Hebrew for Hebrews and that Luke translated it into Greek, which explains its style; Paul left his name off because Hebrews were suspicious of him.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jas
blocks.body:
James reads like Jewish wisdom literature, a series of short exhortations full of vivid images: a wave tossed by the wind, a bridled horse, a ship's rudder, a forest fire. It has more commands per verse than any other New Testament book and more echoes of the Sermon on the Mount (Jas 5:12; Matt 5:34–37).

It defends the poor ("hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith", Jas 2:5), condemns favouritism and denounces rich landowners who withhold wages (Jas 5:4). Its statement that "faith without works is dead" (Jas 2:26) is often contrasted with Paul, but James is attacking a faith that only says the right words (Jas 2:19).

blocks.subject: entry:book/jas
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
James describes God as "the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness" from whom comes "every good gift" (Jas 1:17), and who "of his own will begat he us with the word of truth" (Jas 1:18): a Father who gives birth to his children.

"Pure religion" is to visit "the fatherless and widows in their affliction" (Jas 1:27): to share the Father's heart for those without family. Living faith is union expressing itself in love, the same point Paul makes as "faith which worketh by love" (Gal 5:6). James echoes Jesus' teaching at every turn, so his letter is a picture of what the Sermon on the Mount looks like in community.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jas
blocks.title: James the Lord's brother?
blocks.body:
**For:** the simple opening "James, a servant of God" (Jas 1:1) assumes a well-known James; the letter is very Jewish, close to Jesus' sayings and does not use developed Christian titles. James of Jerusalem was a natural leader for "the twelve tribes" abroad.

**Against:** the Greek is good and stylish, which some think unlikely for a Galilean; the letter was slow to be accepted (Eusebius lists it as disputed); and Jas 2:14–26 is often read as reacting to a later misunderstanding of Paul.

Recent scholarship has become more open to authenticity, since Greek was widely spoken in Galilee and a secretary could have helped. Opinion remains divided.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jas
blocks.title: Eusebius' 'disputed' books
blocks.body: Eusebius, writing in the early 4th century, listed James, Jude, 2 Peter, and 2 and 3 John among the "disputed" books (*antilegomena*): writings known to most churches and read publicly, but not accepted everywhere.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1pe
blocks.body:
1 Peter is addressed to Christians in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, many of them Gentiles, who were facing slander and hostility because they no longer joined in their neighbours' religious and social life (1 Pet 4:3–4). Peter calls them "strangers and pilgrims" (1 Pet 2:11) and gives them Israel's titles: "a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation" (1 Pet 2:9).

The letter blends encouragement, household instruction and reflection on suffering. It contains the puzzling passage about Christ preaching "unto the spirits in prison" (1 Pet 3:19), and closes with greetings from "Babylon" and from Mark (1 Pet 5:13).

blocks.subject: entry:book/1pe
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
God "hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Pet 1:3), so believers call on him as Father (1 Pet 1:17). New birth into a family is the starting point.

Christ "suffered for us, leaving us an example", and "when he was reviled, reviled not again" (1 Pet 2:21–23). He bore our sins "in his own body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness: by whose stripes ye were healed" (1 Pet 2:24): the cross heals and brings us "to God" (1 Pet 3:18). After his death Christ proclaimed his victory even to imprisoned spirits and is now "gone into heaven... angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him" (1 Pet 3:19–22): Christus Victor.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1pe
blocks.title: Peter or a Petrine circle?
blocks.body:
**For Peter:** the letter names him and Silvanus, who may have shaped the Greek (1 Pet 5:12); its closeness to Peter's speeches in Acts and its early use (Polycarp quotes it) support authenticity. "Babylon" for Rome fits Peter's presence there before Nero's persecution.

**Against:** the polished Greek and Septuagint use seem unlikely from a Galilean fisherman; the letter shares many ideas with Paul; and some read the persecution as more widespread than under Nero. Many critical scholars therefore see it as written by a Petrine group in Rome after his death.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2pe
blocks.body:
2 Peter is written as Peter's last testament. It urges readers to add virtue to faith, appeals to the transfiguration (2 Pet 1:16–18), and denounces false teachers (2Pe 2, closely parallel to Jude). Chapter 3 answers scoffers who say Christ's promised coming has failed: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years" (2 Pet 3:8), and the Lord is patient, "not willing that any should perish" (2 Pet 3:9).

It was among the most debated New Testament books in the early church and is absent from several early lists. It is the only New Testament book to call Paul's letters "scriptures" (2 Pet 3:16).

blocks.subject: entry:book/2pe
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
2 Peter contains the boldest statement of union with God in the New Testament: through his promises we become "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Pet 1:4). Eastern Christianity calls this *theosis*: sharing in the life of the Trinity by grace, the goal of salvation.

God's patience is the Father's longing: "not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance" (2 Pet 3:9). Partial-preterist readers note that the "heavens" and "elements" passing away (2 Pet 3:10–12) echo prophetic language for the end of an old covenant world order, followed by "new heavens and a new earth, wherein dwelleth righteousness" (2 Pet 3:13); others read it of the final renewal. Either way, the promise is a world set right, not an escape from it.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2pe
blocks.title: Is 2 Peter by Peter?
blocks.body:
2 Peter is the New Testament book most widely regarded as pseudonymous, including by many evangelical scholars, though others defend it.

**For Peter:** it claims to be from Peter, an eyewitness of the transfiguration who knows his death is near (2 Pet 1:14–18), and differences from 1 Peter could come from different secretaries.

**Against:** its elaborate Greek differs sharply from 1 Peter; it seems to use Jude; it speaks of Paul's letters as a collection of "scriptures"; it refers to the passing of "the fathers" (2 Pet 3:4); and its acceptance was slow and disputed.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2pe
blocks.title: Origen on 2 Peter
blocks.body: Origen, as reported by Eusebius, said that Peter left one acknowledged letter and perhaps a second, but that the second was disputed.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2pe
blocks.title: Eusebius' 'disputed' books
blocks.body: Eusebius, writing in the early 4th century, listed 2 Peter, along with James, Jude and 2 and 3 John, among the "disputed" books (*antilegomena*): writings known to most churches and read publicly, but not accepted everywhere.

blocks.subject: entry:book/1jn
blocks.body:
1 John has no greeting or signature; it reads like a sermon. It opens by stressing that the "Word of life" was heard, seen and touched (1 John 1:1), against those who denied that Christ came in the flesh. It gives tests of genuine faith: walking in the light, keeping his commands, loving one another, confessing Jesus Christ come in the flesh.

Its high point is "God is love" (1 John 4:8, 16). The famous "three heavenly witnesses" (1 John 5:7–8 in the KJV) are not in the early Greek manuscripts and are absent from modern translations; see the essay "From manuscripts to your Bible".

blocks.subject: entry:book/1jn
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
The purpose of the letter is relational: "that ye also may have fellowship with us: and truly our fellowship is with the Father, and with his Son Jesus Christ" (1 John 1:3). The gospel is invitation into the communion of the Trinity.

"Behold, what manner of love the Father hath bestowed upon us, that we should be called the sons of God" (1 John 3:1). God is love, and "herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son" (1 John 4:10). Christ is the *hilasmos* for our sins, "and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world" (1 John 2:2), the means by which sin is cleansed and fellowship restored. "For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil" (1 John 3:8). Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

blocks.subject: entry:book/1jn
blocks.title: Who wrote the letters of John?
blocks.body: 1 John is anonymous; 2 and 3 John come from "the elder". Their vocabulary and themes are close to John's Gospel (light, life, love, abiding, truth). Tradition from Irenaeus onward assigned all of them to the apostle John. Many scholars think "the elder" was a leader of the Johannine community, possibly the "John the Elder" whom Papias mentions as distinct from the apostle. Eusebius listed 2 and 3 John among the disputed books. Most date the letters after the Gospel, c. 90–110.

blocks.subject: entry:book/2jn
blocks.body: 2 John is about the length of a single sheet of papyrus. "The elder" writes to "the elect lady and her children", most likely a congregation. He commends those "walking in truth", repeats Jesus' command to love one another, and warns against welcoming travelling teachers who deny "that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh" (2 John 1:7). He hopes to visit and speak "face to face" (2 John 1:12).

blocks.subject: entry:book/2jn
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body: Truth and love belong together because both are found in a person: Jesus, the Father's Son, who came in real flesh (2 John 1:3, 7). Denying the incarnation is denying that God has truly joined himself to humanity, and so cutting off the very union by which we are saved. The elder's longing to speak "face to face, that our joy may be full" (2 John 1:12) echoes the relational goal of the gospel.

blocks.subject: entry:book/3jn
blocks.body: 3 John is the shortest book in the Bible by word count in Greek. The elder thanks Gaius for welcoming travelling missionaries who went out "for his name's sake, taking nothing of the Gentiles" (3 John 1:7), so that "we might be fellowhelpers to the truth". He criticises Diotrephes, a local leader who refused to receive the elder's messengers and expelled those who did, and commends Demetrius, probably the letter-carrier.

blocks.subject: entry:book/3jn
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body: Hospitality makes us "fellowhelpers to the truth" (3 John 1:8): sharing in Christ's mission by opening our homes. The contrast between Gaius and Diotrephes, "who loveth to have the preeminence" (3 John 1:9), is the contrast Jesus drew between rulers who lord it over others and the Son of Man who came to serve (Mark 10:42–45). "He that doeth good is of God" (3 John 1:11).

blocks.subject: entry:book/jud
blocks.body:
Jude meant to write about "the common salvation" but had to warn against intruders who "turn the grace of our God into lasciviousness" (Jude 1:3–4). He piles up examples from Israel's history and Jewish tradition: the wilderness generation, angels who left their place, Sodom, Cain, Balaam and Korah.

Jude cites 1 Enoch (Jude 1:14–15) and alludes to a tradition about Michael and the devil disputing over Moses' body (Jude 1:9), probably from the Assumption of Moses. This use of non-canonical Jewish writings made some early Christians hesitate over the letter. It shares much material with 2 Peter 2.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jud
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Jude is addressed "to them that are sanctified by God the Father, and preserved in Jesus Christ, and called" (Jude 1:1): held by the Father and the Son. Its practical heart is "Keep yourselves in the love of God, looking for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Jude 1:21), and to rescue others with mercy (Jude 1:22–23).

It ends with a doxology of confidence: "unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy" (Jude 1:24). The goal is presence and joy.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jud
blocks.title: Jude, brother of James?
blocks.body: The author calls himself "the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James" (Jude 1:1), naturally Jude the brother of Jesus. Many scholars argue no forger would choose so obscure a figure, and the letter's Jewish apocalyptic world fits early Palestinian Christianity. Others think its Greek and its reference to the apostles' words as past (Jude 1:17) point to a later writer. Its use of 1 Enoch troubled some early readers, and Eusebius counted it among the disputed books.

blocks.subject: entry:book/jud
blocks.title: Eusebius' 'disputed' books
blocks.body: Eusebius, writing in the early 4th century, listed Jude, together with James, 2 Peter and 2 and 3 John, among the "disputed" books (*antilegomena*): writings known to most churches and read publicly, but not accepted everywhere.

blocks.subject: entry:book/rev
blocks.body:
Revelation is a letter to seven real churches in Asia (Rev 2–3), framed as prophecy and written in the apocalyptic style of Daniel and Ezekiel. Symbolism is everywhere: numbers (seven, twelve, 666), creatures, colours, cities. John is "in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ" (Rev 1:9).

After the letters, John sees God's throne and a Lamb "as it had been slain" (Rev 5:6). Seven seals, trumpets and bowls of judgment follow; a dragon and two beasts make war on the saints; Babylon the great falls. A rider called Faithful and True defeats the beast with the sword from his mouth (Rev 19:11–21); Satan is bound for a thousand years (Rev 20); and the new Jerusalem comes down from heaven, where God "will dwell with them" and wipe away every tear (Rev 21:3–4).

Four main schools of interpretation exist: preterist (mostly fulfilled in the first century), historicist (church history), futurist (mostly future) and idealist (timeless symbols); many readers blend them.

blocks.subject: entry:book/rev
blocks.title: Reading it through Christ
blocks.body:
Revelation is "the Revelation of Jesus Christ" (Rev 1:1): it unveils him. John hears of "the Lion of the tribe of Juda" and turns to see a slain Lamb (Rev 5:5–6). God's power is revealed as self-giving love; the Lamb conquers by his blood and his followers overcome "by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony" (Rev 12:11). The rider's only weapon is the sword from his mouth (Rev 19:15): the word of the gospel.

A partial-preterist reading, which this app follows, takes the time markers seriously ("must shortly come to pass", Rev 1:1; "the time is at hand", Rev 1:3) and reads much of the book as the judgment of the old covenant order and the persecuting powers of the first century, with Jerusalem's fall in AD 70 and Rome's power in view. The thousand years (Rev 20) is the reign of Christ now, during which the gospel advances and the nations are discipled. The new Jerusalem is the bride (Rev 21:2, 9–10), already descending and to be consummated, where "the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations" (Rev 22:2). The goal is God dwelling with humanity: "they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them" (Rev 21:3).

blocks.subject: entry:book/rev
blocks.title: Before AD 70 or under Domitian?
blocks.body:
This question matters because preterist readings depend on it.

**Late date, c. 95 (majority):** Irenaeus places John's vision at the end of Domitian's reign, and Eusebius follows him. The letters show churches that have had time to grow and decline (Ephesus has "left thy first love", Rev 2:4; Laodicea is rich, though it was damaged by an earthquake in AD 60). Emperor worship in Asia was well developed under Domitian. "Babylon" as a name for Rome is common in Jewish writings after AD 70.

**Early date, c. 64–69 (minority):** John is told to measure the temple and the outer court that will be trampled for 42 months (Rev 11:1–2), which assumes the temple stands. Of seven kings, "five are fallen, and one is" (Rev 17:10), which fits Nero (or Galba) if counted from Julius or Augustus. The number 666 matches "Nero Caesar" in Hebrew letters, and a variant reading 616 matches the Latin spelling. The repeated "shortly" fits a near crisis. J. A. T. Robinson, in *Redating the New Testament*, and several preterist writers argue for this date.

Some also note that Domitian's persecution is less well attested than once thought.

blocks.subject: entry:book/rev
blocks.title: Irenaeus: seen near the end of Domitian's reign
blocks.body: Irenaeus, discussing the number of the beast, said that if the name were meant to be announced plainly it would have been by the one who saw the apocalyptic vision, for it was seen not long ago, almost in our own generation, toward the end of Domitian's reign. This is the main external evidence for the late date. Some early-date advocates argue that "it was seen" could refer to John himself rather than the vision, but most scholars take it of the vision.

blocks.subject: entry:book/rev
blocks.title: Which John?
blocks.body: The author calls himself John four times (Rev 1:1, 4, 9; 22:8) but never claims to be an apostle. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus identified him with the apostle. Already in the 3rd century, Dionysius of Alexandria argued on grounds of style that he was a different John. Eusebius suggested the "elder John" mentioned by Papias. Most scholars today speak of "John of Patmos", a prophet distinct from the author of the Gospel, though some still defend apostolic authorship and note shared imagery (the Word, the Lamb, living water).

blocks.subject: entry:book/rev
blocks.title: Dionysius of Alexandria on style
blocks.body: Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria in the 3rd century, accepted Revelation as the work of a holy and inspired man named John, but argued from its vocabulary, style and grammar that it was not written by the same John who wrote the Gospel and 1 John.

blocks.subject: entry:book/rev
blocks.title: Augustine: the thousand years are now
blocks.body: Augustine taught that the binding of Satan and the thousand years of Rev 20 describe the present age of the church, from Christ's first coming, and that the "first resurrection" is the spiritual resurrection of believers now. This amillennial reading became standard in the Western church.

blocks.subject: entry:book/rev
blocks.title: Warfield: the millennium and the intermediate state
blocks.body: B. B. Warfield, a postmillennialist in his view of history, argued that the "thousand years" of Rev 20 is a picture of the blessedness of the saints with Christ in heaven during the intermediate state, not an earthly era. He nonetheless expected the gospel to triumph across the earth before Christ's return, drawing on Rev 19:11–21 as a picture of the victory of the gospel.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/nt-dating
blocks.title: What is certain
blocks.body:
Some anchor points are secure. Jesus' ministry and crucifixion fall under Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea from AD 26 to 36. The Gallio inscription at Delphi places Paul in Corinth around AD 51–52 (Acts 18:12). Paul's undisputed letters were written in the 50s. Nero's persecution in Rome followed the fire of AD 64. The Romans destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in AD 70.

James the Lord's brother was executed in AD 62, which Josephus reports. Clement of Rome's letter to Corinth (c. AD 96) and Ignatius' letters (c. AD 110) already use several New Testament writings, setting a latest possible date for those books.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/nt-dating
blocks.title: The case for early dating
blocks.body:
A minority of scholars argue that every New Testament book was written before AD 70. Their main arguments:

1. **Acts stops in AD 62.** It ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome for two years (Acts 28:30–31). It does not mention Nero's persecution (64), the deaths of James (62), Peter or Paul, or Jerusalem's fall. If Acts was written c. 62–64, Luke was earlier, and Mark (used by Luke) earlier still.
2. **Silence about the temple's destruction.** The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 was a catastrophe for Judaism and early Christianity. No New Testament book refers to it as a past event, even where it would strengthen the argument, as in Hebrews' claim that the old sacrifices are obsolete (Heb 8:13; 10:1–2).
3. **Jesus' prophecies read as genuine prediction.** Mat 24, Mrk 13 and Luk 21 speak of the temple's ruin within "this generation". Early-daters argue these texts lack the specific details one would expect if written after the event.
4. **Present-tense descriptions** of Jerusalem and the temple (John 5:2; Heb 8:4; Rev 11:1–2).

This view is marked **minority**. It is important to partial-preterist readings of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/nt-dating
blocks.title: J. A. T. Robinson's Redating the New Testament
blocks.body: John A. T. Robinson, a liberal Anglican scholar and not a conservative apologist, argued in *Redating the New Testament* (1976) that the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 is never mentioned as past in any New Testament book, and that this silence is best explained if all of them were written before it. He placed the whole New Testament, including John and Revelation, between about AD 47 and 70. His book drew wide attention but did not change the majority view.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/nt-dating
blocks.title: Counter-arguments and the majority view
blocks.body:
Most scholars accept early dates for Paul's undisputed letters but place the Gospels and several other books later:

- **Mark** c. 65–73; **Matthew** and **Luke** c. 80–90 (they use Mark); **Acts** c. 80–90 (some later); **John** c. 90–100; **Revelation** c. 95; disputed letters (Pastorals, 2 Peter) from c. 80 to as late as c. 130.

Their replies to the early-dating arguments:

- **Acts' ending** is literary. Its story is about the gospel reaching Rome "no man forbidding him" (Acts 28:31). Paul's farewell speech already anticipates his death (Acts 20:25, 38).
- **Silence about AD 70** is an argument from silence. Matthew's parable of the king who "burned up their city" (Matt 22:7) and Luke's "Jerusalem compassed with armies" (Luke 21:20) are read by many as reflecting the event.
- **Development**: some scholars see later church structures, theology and a cooling of end-time urgency in certain books.
- **External evidence**: Irenaeus dates Revelation to Domitian's reign (Against Heresies 5.30.3).

Some critics also assume predictive prophecy cannot explain detailed foreknowledge; early-daters reply that this is a philosophical assumption rather than evidence.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/nt-dating
blocks.title: Manuscript evidence
blocks.body:
The surviving manuscripts set latest possible dates and show how quickly the books spread. Dates are assigned mainly by handwriting style (palaeography), which gives ranges, not exact years.

| Manuscript | Contents | Generally accepted date | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P52** (Rylands Library) | John 18:31–33, 37–38 | c. AD 125–175 | Long called the oldest New Testament fragment, often dated "c. 125". Some papyrologists argue for a wider range reaching into the 3rd century (**disputed**). |
| **P46** (Chester Beatty) | Paul's letters and Hebrews | c. AD 175–225 (usually "c. 200") | A proposed late-1st-century date has found almost no support (**minority**). Places Hebrews after Romans. |
| **P66** (Bodmer II) | Much of John | c. AD 175–225 | Some argue for the mid-2nd century, others for the 3rd (**disputed**). |
| **P75** (Bodmer XIV–XV) | Luke and John | c. AD 175–225 | Text very close to Codex Vaticanus; some propose a 4th-century date (**minority**). |
| **Codex Sinaiticus** | Whole New Testament, much of the Old Testament | c. AD 330–360 | Found at St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, in the 19th century. |
| **Codex Vaticanus** | Most of the Bible (end of New Testament lost) | c. AD 300–350 | In the Vatican Library since at least the 15th century. |

None of these copies can prove an early or late date of composition, since originals were written before them. But P52 in Egypt, if dated in the 2nd century, shows John was circulating well before AD 150, which rules out the very late dates once proposed for John by some 19th-century critics.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/nt-dating
blocks.title: What depends on the dates
blocks.body:
- **Eyewitness distance.** On the majority view, Mark was written about 35–40 years after Jesus' death, within the lifetime of eyewitnesses; on the early view, about 30 years or less. Either way the gap is short compared with most ancient biographies.
- **Reading prophecy.** If the Gospels were written before 70, Jesus' predictions of Jerusalem's fall stand as prophecy fulfilled within "this generation" (Matt 24:34). If Revelation was written before 70, a preterist reading of much of it becomes more natural.
- **Authorship.** Early dates make apostolic or close-associate authorship easier to hold; late dates often go with pseudonymity.

The gospel's truth does not rest on any one dating scheme; the resurrection was being proclaimed in Jerusalem within weeks of the crucifixion, and Paul passes on a creed he "received" within a few years of it (1 Cor 15:3–8).

blocks.subject: entry:essay/nt-dating
blocks.title: Why this app leans early on some books
blocks.body:
This app's partial-preterist reading takes Jesus' time-statements at face value: "this generation shall not pass" (Matt 24:34), "there be some standing here, which shall not taste of death" (Matt 16:28), "things which must shortly come to pass" (Rev 1:1). Those statements fit best if the Gospels and Revelation were written before AD 70, as warnings of a judgment still to come.

We present that as a **minority** scholarly position, not a settled fact, and show the majority view alongside it. What matters most is not the date but the event: in AD 70 the old covenant order of temple and sacrifice ended, and the kingdom that "cannot be moved" (Heb 12:28) continued to grow.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: What 'canon' means
blocks.body: "Canon" comes from a Greek word for a measuring rod. Applied to Scripture, it means the list of books a community recognises as its authoritative rule. The process was gradual. Churches did not so much create the canon as recognise writings already in use, testing them by apostolic origin, agreement with the rule of faith, and wide, long-standing use in worship.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: The Old Testament: Law, Prophets, Writings
blocks.body:
The Hebrew Bible (*Tanakh*) has three parts: the **Torah** (Law), the **Nevi'im** (Prophets: Joshua–Kings and Isaiah–Malachi, without Daniel) and the **Ketuvim** (Writings: Psalms, Proverbs, Job, the five scrolls, Daniel, Ezra–Nehemiah, Chronicles). Its 24 books contain the same text as the Protestant Old Testament's 39; the difference is how they are counted (the twelve minor prophets are one book, Samuel, Kings and Chronicles are one each, and Ezra–Nehemiah is one).

Signs of the three-part shape appear early. The prologue to Sirach (c. 132 BC) refers to "the Law and the Prophets and the other books". Jesus speaks of "the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms" (Luke 24:44), and of the blood "from Abel to Zacharias" (Luke 11:51), perhaps the first and last murders in the Hebrew order, which ends with Chronicles (2 Chr 24:20–21). The Talmud gives the traditional order of the Prophets and Writings and their authors.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: Josephus: twenty-two books
blocks.body: Josephus, writing in the 90s AD, says the Jews do not have countless conflicting books but only twenty-two, justly believed: five books of Moses; thirteen books of the prophets covering history from Moses to Artaxerxes; and four books of hymns to God and precepts for life. He says that books written after Artaxerxes are not held in the same esteem because the exact succession of prophets had ceased. His count of 22 probably joins Ruth to Judges and Lamentations to Jeremiah.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: Melito's list
blocks.body: Melito of Sardis travelled to the East to learn accurately which books belonged to the Old Testament and sent a list to a friend named Onesimus. It matches the Hebrew canon but omits Esther (and does not separately name Lamentations or Nehemiah, probably counted with Jeremiah and Ezra). It is the earliest surviving Christian list of Old Testament books.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: The 'Council of Jamnia' hypothesis
blocks.body:
For much of the 20th century textbooks taught that a Jewish "Council of Jamnia" (Yavneh) around AD 90 closed the Hebrew canon. The idea goes back to 19th-century scholarship.

Scholars now widely reject this picture. There was a rabbinic academy at Yavneh after AD 70, and the Mishnah records discussions there about whether Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs "defile the hands" (are sacred Scripture). But there was no council in the church sense, no binding decree, and the discussions concerned books already widely accepted. Debates over books such as Esther, Ecclesiastes and Ezekiel continued afterwards. Most scholars now think the Hebrew canon was largely settled in practice before the first century AD, or that it settled gradually and was not "closed" by any single act.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: The New Testament: a gradual recognition
blocks.body:
The earliest Christians' Bible was the Jewish Scriptures, usually in Greek. Alongside them, the words of Jesus and the letters of apostles were read in worship (Col 4:16; 1 Thess 5:27). By the time 2 Peter was written, Paul's letters were already being collected and compared with "the other scriptures" (2 Pet 3:15–16).

By about AD 180 the four Gospels, Acts, the thirteen Pauline letters, 1 Peter and 1 John were widely accepted. Irenaeus argues that there must be four Gospels, no more and no fewer. Disputes continued over Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude and Revelation, and some churches also read writings such as the Shepherd of Hermas, 1 Clement and the Didache. Challenges sharpened the process: Marcion (c. 140) accepted only an edited Luke and ten of Paul's letters.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: The Muratorian fragment
blocks.body:
The Muratorian fragment is a Latin list of New Testament books, damaged at the start, discovered by Ludovico Antonio Muratori and published in 1740. It accepts four Gospels (Luke and John named; Matthew and Mark lost in the damaged opening), Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, Jude, two letters of John, the Wisdom of Solomon and the Revelations of John and of Peter (adding that some will not let the latter be read in church). It rejects letters forged in Paul's name for Marcion and says the Shepherd of Hermas may be read privately but not publicly, because it was written recently. It does not mention Hebrews, James or the letters of Peter (except the Apocalypse).

**Date (contested):** most scholars date it to the late 2nd century, around AD 170–200, because it calls Hermas recent. A minority argue for a 4th-century Eastern origin.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: Eusebius' three categories
blocks.body:
Around AD 325 Eusebius sorted the books into categories:

- **Recognised** (*homologoumena*): the four Gospels, Acts, Paul's letters (in which he included Hebrews), 1 John, 1 Peter and, "if it seem proper", Revelation.
- **Disputed** (*antilegomena*), but known to most: James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John.
- **Spurious** (*notha*): books such as the Acts of Paul, the Shepherd of Hermas, the Apocalypse of Peter, Barnabas and the Didache, and, he says, perhaps Revelation for some.

He also named heretical books, such as the Gospels of Peter and Thomas, to be rejected entirely.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: Athanasius' Thirty-Ninth Festal Letter (AD 367)
blocks.body: In his Easter letter of 367, Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, listed the twenty-seven books of our New Testament, the first surviving list to match it exactly. He called them "the springs of salvation". For the Old Testament he listed the Hebrew books (with Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah attached to Jeremiah, and without Esther), and named the Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the Didache and the Shepherd as books to be read by new converts, though not canonical.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: Councils
blocks.body:
- **Hippo (393)** and **Carthage (397, and again 419):** regional North African councils, influenced by Augustine, listed the 27 New Testament books and an Old Testament that included Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach and 1–2 Maccabees. These were local decisions, not binding on the whole church.
- **Trent (1546):** in response to the Reformation, the Council of Trent's fourth session (8 April 1546) defined the Catholic canon, including the deuterocanonical books, as dogma for the Roman Catholic Church.
- **Protestant confessions:** the Westminster Confession (1646, ch. 1) lists the 66 books and excludes the Apocrypha; the Church of England's Thirty-Nine Articles (Article 6) allows the Apocrypha to be read "for example of life" but not to establish doctrine.
- **Orthodox:** the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) affirmed several deuterocanonical books; Orthodox churches have not defined a single closed list in the same way.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: Jerome and Augustine disagree
blocks.body: Jerome, translating the Old Testament from Hebrew, held that books outside the Hebrew canon should be set apart as "apocrypha"; the church could read them for edification but not use them to establish doctrine. He set this out in his preface to Samuel and Kings, the "helmeted prologue".

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: Augustine's wider list
blocks.body: Augustine listed the canonical books including Tobit, Judith, 1–2 Maccabees, Wisdom and Sirach, and advised readers to prefer books received by all churches, then those received by the more numerous and weightier churches.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: Apocrypha and deuterocanon
blocks.body:
The books in question are Tobit, Judith, 1 and 2 Maccabees, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus), Baruch (with the Letter of Jeremiah), and additions to Esther and Daniel (the Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three, Susanna, Bel and the Dragon). Catholics call them **deuterocanonical** ("second canon"), recognised as Scripture later than the others. Protestants call them **Apocrypha**. Orthodox Bibles also include 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, Psalm 151 and the Prayer of Manasseh, with 4 Maccabees in an appendix in some.

These books were written c. 300 BC–AD 100, mostly in Greek or surviving in Greek, and were included in manuscripts of the Septuagint used by the early church. They are not in the Hebrew Bible. The New Testament never quotes them as Scripture, though it echoes some (compare Heb 11:35 with 2 Maccabees 7). Luther's 1534 German Bible printed them in a separate section between the Testaments, and the 1611 King James Version also included them in a separate section.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: Why Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox canons differ
blocks.body:
All three traditions share the same 27-book New Testament. The difference is the Old Testament.

- **Protestants** follow the Hebrew canon (Jerome's view): what the Jewish people received as Scripture, which Jesus and the apostles used, and which Josephus describes.
- **Catholics** follow the wider canon used in the Greek-speaking early church and confirmed at Hippo and Carthage and defined at Trent, arguing that the church's long liturgical use counts.
- **Orthodox** follow the Septuagint tradition, with a slightly larger collection and less emphasis on a single dogmatically closed list.

Each side can point to early witnesses: Melito, Athanasius and Jerome on one side; Augustine and the North African councils on the other. The disagreement is real, but the shared core of Scripture is very large, and all three traditions read the whole through Christ.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/canon
blocks.title: The canon and the Son
blocks.body:
Jesus said the Scriptures "testify of me" (John 5:39) and on the road to Emmaus opened "all the scriptures the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27). The church recognised books as canonical largely by asking whether they bore faithful witness to him.

That gives a key for reading the canon too: Jesus is the centre that holds the collection together. He is God's final Word (Heb 1:1–2), the clearest picture of the Father, and every part of Scripture is read in his light.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/manuscripts
blocks.title: No originals, many copies
blocks.body:
None of the original manuscripts (autographs) of any biblical book survives. What we have are copies of copies: more than 5,000 Greek New Testament manuscripts, from small papyrus fragments to complete Bibles, plus thousands of early translations (Latin, Syriac, Coptic) and quotations by early Christian writers. No other ancient text comes close to this number or to how near the earliest copies are to the time of writing.

Copyists made mistakes: skipped lines, misread letters, harmonised one Gospel with another, or added clarifying words. Textual criticism compares the copies to work out the earliest recoverable wording. The great majority of variants are spelling or word-order differences that do not affect meaning or translation.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/manuscripts
blocks.title: The Old Testament text
blocks.body:
- **Masoretic Text:** the standard Hebrew text, preserved by Jewish scribes called Masoretes (c. AD 600–1000), who added vowel signs and notes. Its best complete witnesses are the Aleppo Codex (c. AD 930, now partly damaged) and the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008/1009), the basis of modern printed Hebrew Bibles.
- **Dead Sea Scrolls:** found from 1947 at Qumran, including fragments of every Old Testament book except Esther, from c. 250 BC to AD 68. The Great Isaiah Scroll (c. 2nd century BC) is about a thousand years older than the Leningrad Codex and largely agrees with it.
- **Septuagint:** the Greek translation made from the 3rd century BC, used by the early church. In places (e.g. Jeremiah) it reflects a different Hebrew edition.
- **Samaritan Pentateuch:** the Samaritan community's Torah, with some deliberate and some accidental differences.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/manuscripts
blocks.title: Text-types (families)
blocks.body:
New Testament manuscripts are grouped by shared readings into broad "text-types":

- **Alexandrian:** associated with Egypt, found in the early papyri (P66, P75) and Codex Vaticanus and Sinaiticus. Generally shorter and less smoothed. Most textual critics regard it as closest to the originals.
- **Western:** found in Codex Bezae (c. AD 400), Old Latin versions and some early writers. Known for paraphrase and additions, especially in Acts, which is nearly a tenth longer in Bezae.
- **Byzantine:** the text of the great majority of later Greek manuscripts, standard in the Greek-speaking church from about the 9th century. Fuller and smoother, combining readings.
- **Caesarean:** a proposed group for Mark, now widely doubted as a distinct family.

Many scholars now use more precise computer-based methods (the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method) behind the newest editions, and see "text-types" as useful but simplified.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/manuscripts
blocks.title: The great codices
blocks.body:
A codex is a book with pages rather than a scroll. The great 4th–5th-century parchment codices are the earliest complete or near-complete Bibles:

- **Codex Vaticanus (B):** c. AD 300–350; in the Vatican Library. Missing the end of Hebrews onward (the Pastorals, Philemon and Revelation).
- **Codex Sinaiticus (א, Aleph):** c. AD 330–360; found at St Catherine's Monastery, Sinai, by Constantin von Tischendorf (1844 and 1859); most now in the British Library. The oldest complete New Testament; also contains the Epistle of Barnabas and part of the Shepherd of Hermas.
- **Codex Alexandrinus (A):** c. AD 400–440; British Library. Mixed text: Byzantine in the Gospels, Alexandrian elsewhere. Contains 1 and 2 Clement.
- **Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus (C):** 5th century; a palimpsest, its biblical text scraped off and overwritten with sermons of Ephrem the Syrian.
- **Codex Bezae (D):** c. AD 400; Greek and Latin on facing pages; the main Western witness.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/manuscripts
blocks.title: The Textus Receptus
blocks.body:
The first printed Greek New Testament published was Erasmus' edition of 1516. Erasmus used a handful of late medieval Byzantine manuscripts available in Basel. For the last verses of Revelation, missing in his manuscript, he translated back from the Latin Vulgate, and a few readings in his text are found in no Greek manuscript.

His text was revised by Stephanus (1550, the first edition with verse numbers in 1551) and Beza. An Elzevir edition of 1633 advertised it as "the text now received by all", from which comes the name **Textus Receptus** ("received text"). The translators of the King James Version (1611) worked mainly from Beza's and Stephanus' editions.

From the 18th century onward, editors such as Lachmann, Tischendorf, Tregelles, and Westcott and Hort (1881) built "critical texts" on the older manuscripts. Today's standard editions are the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece* (28th edition) and the United Bible Societies' *Greek New Testament* (5th edition), which underlie most modern translations.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/manuscripts
blocks.title: Why some KJV verses are missing from modern Bibles
blocks.body:
When a modern Bible jumps from, say, Matt 17:20 to Matt 17:22, the verse has not been deleted by a modern translator: it is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is judged to be a later addition, so it is placed in a footnote. Verse numbers were fixed in the 16th century from the Textus Receptus, so a gap appears.

Verses commonly footnoted: Matt 17:21; 18:11; 23:14; Mark 7:16; 9:44; 9:46; 11:26; 15:28; Luke 17:36; 23:17; John 5:4; Acts 8:37; 15:34; 24:7; 28:29; Rom 16:24. Many are harmonisations, where a scribe copied a phrase from a parallel passage (e.g. Matt 18:11 from Luke 19:10).

Two longer passages are usually kept but bracketed:

- **The longer ending of Mark (Mark 16:9–20):** absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; known by the 2nd century (Irenaeus quotes Mark 16:19).
- **The woman caught in adultery (John 7:53–8:11):** absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; some manuscripts place it elsewhere in John or in Luke. Many scholars think it is a genuine early story about Jesus that was not originally part of John.

The **Comma Johanneum** (1 John 5:7–8, "the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one") appears in no Greek manuscript before the medieval period and in only a handful at all, mostly in margins. It entered Latin manuscripts and Erasmus' third edition (1522). Modern Bibles omit it. The Trinity is taught elsewhere (Matt 28:19; 2 Cor 13:14) and never depended on this verse.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/manuscripts
blocks.title: Critical text or received text?
blocks.body:
**Majority of textual scholars (reasoned eclecticism):** the earliest manuscripts generally preserve the earliest text; scribes tended to add rather than remove; each variant is weighed by external evidence (age, spread and quality of manuscripts) and internal evidence (which reading best explains the others). This produces the Nestle–Aland and UBS texts.

**Byzantine priority / Majority Text (minority):** some scholars argue that the text found in most manuscripts is likely the original, since it was copied most widely in the church that used Greek continuously; the early Alexandrian manuscripts may represent a local, edited text that survived because of Egypt's dry climate.

**Textus Receptus / KJV-only positions (minority):** some Christians hold that God providentially preserved the text in the Textus Receptus, or in the King James Version specifically. Textual scholars across the theological spectrum, including most evangelicals, do not accept this, since the TR rests on a few late manuscripts and contains readings with no Greek support.

What all sides agree: the differences affect a small fraction of the text, and no core Christian teaching depends on a disputed reading.

blocks.subject: entry:essay/manuscripts
blocks.title: Trusting the text, following the Word
blocks.body:
The Bible's textual history is messy and human, and that is not a threat. God chose to speak through human words, copied by human hands, just as the Word himself took flesh. The abundance of manuscripts means we can know the text with remarkable confidence, and honest footnotes are a mark of care, not of loss.

Scripture's authority does not rest on a perfect chain of copies but on the One it bears witness to. The written word leads us to the living Word, "the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person" (Heb 1:3).
